utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vezmarovic. I was going through yesterday's transcript, and I realised that the interpreters had to warn us a number of times. I do feel to some degree responsible, because perhaps I wasn't focusing enough on that aspect. So I would like to ask you to moderate your speed when testifying, please, sir. On the first day of your testimony you described to the OTP - we're talking about the 20th now, let there be no mistake about that - noticing men among the prisoners who wore bandages, and you said there were about 70 per cent of those that were, in fact, wearing bandages. When the OTP asked you whether any medical assistance was provided to those people, you said there wasn't. My question: Did either you or your soldiers check during your time in the hangar if those injuries were faked or real? Did any of those soldiers actually address you or your soldiers, seeking some form of medical assistance at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the time I first got there and the time I withdrew, nobody asked anything. But that was something that happened at another time, perhaps, but at that point in time I don't think anybody sought medical assistance, nor did we check their injuries to see what their injuries were like. I simply had them moved to one side, and tried to guard them properly. Everything else that I was going to do at a later stage was eventually not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You further described that you gave approval for local, if I may call them that, TO men, to enter in groups. You said there was bad language being used. So I inferred that you were, in fact, able to hear the comments they were making. While those locals were touring the inside of the hangar, did you hear any of them make any remarks to that effect, that the injuries were fake, that the bandages were just being used to conceal the fact that there were no injuries? Did you hear anything like that being said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember in particular what people were saying. I didn't talk to them directly. I wasn't eavesdropping or anything. I heard things in passing. I would catch snippets of their conversation, but it wasn't as if I was actually talking to any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Let me now return to the final part of your testimony. But before I do that, I will ask you several questions about something we already talked about yesterday to do with the regulations that I asked you about. Please try to provide brief answers. Do you agree with me that, based on the rules of service pertaining to the military police, the ones that we went through yesterday, you, as a commander of an independent military police company, would have and should have been under the command of your brigade commander only and nobody else? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to what the rules of service actually say, in that case you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely my question. Based on the same rules of service, could you possibly have been under the command of a senior officer - senior to you, I mean, in terms of position and rank - from your own brigade, but only having received special authorisation from the brigade commander himself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember the rules of service and what I was actually taught and trained for, security organ could in theory have exercised command over the military police, but again, as far as I remember, it could not possibly have been a signals officer or an engineer, for example. That's what I remember, which doesn't necessarily mean that my recollection is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that any order that wasn't issued to you by the brigade commander himself was not binding for you until such time as you received approval or consent from your brigade commander, your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've cast the net pretty wide there, I think. As a matter of principle, I don't think you're right. Why am I saying this? There were times people called me to step in regarding problems about certain soldiers. That would be an example of a very general situation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean problems with a soldier, that would be in the line of your regular duties, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about receiving information from the duty officer in your company at certain times. But you also talked about receiving orders from the duty officer of the brigade. Will you agree with me that the company duty officer and the brigade duty officer could, at the very most, only have conveyed orders from your superior to you but not actually give you orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how successful I was in explaining this yesterday, but what you're asking me now is exactly what you can find in the rules of service. This is how it should always be, and this is how we practiced it at various drills. However, both the drills and the manual itself containing the rules of service were drafted with the assumption of a defensive war in mind. This time around we were facing a totally different reality. The situation was quite different. And with all due respect for the rules, we had to cope the best we could. However, at no point in time did we stray from the rules altogether. If you keep in mind all the principles that an officer must abide by, one of those is his determination or decisiveness to act in a certain situation, as he sees fit. If you want us to stick to the rules of service and not stray at all, this wasn't something that you could always apply out there in the field. At least, not all the elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you submit reports to your superiors whenever there were deviations or aberrations from those rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I did start writing reports, and I set out with the best intention to comply with all the rules. There were, however, as it turned out, it wasn't quite possible to keep up with that on a daily basis because of all the tasks facing us, all the duties. The reports at the outset were daily reports, and then I would submit them every other day. Sometimes there would be two reports a day, with a one-day delay. And later on they ceased for a while, and I think it was towards the end of my time there when I was already at the barracks that I resumed these reports. You keep confusing me by invoking the rules of service. When Lieutenant Jeftic came, he was the officer that I talked to, he was the officer directing me and in some way, if you like, giving me orders, including an obligation, whenever I sent out a military police patrol, to write down all the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, I'm sorry I have to interrupt you. This is all fine. You have said it before, but please can you give me a specific answer. If you noticed any deviations from the rules, or whenever you noticed deviations from the rules, did you produce and submit a written report or even an oral one? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness should be allowed to answer the question properly. Not always just be fettered by "yes" and "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to say this: I don't think I strayed from the rules at any point in time. There was this period of time when I wasn't submitting any reports, but I was convinced that I was doing the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Surely you must know that, under the rules of service, if a decision of a superior -- if the decision of an officer is changed by a superior officer, under Rule 41 of the rules of service in the armed forces, the superior must inform the officer who originally issued the order, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there is such a thing as initiative. If there is a particularly complex situation on the ground, an officer is entitled to change the method by which an assignment is carried out, but not the objective itself. As long as I complied with that, I think I was still on the safe side, because that's what I had been taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for as long as you keep your superior informed of any changes, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to know if I made any mistakes and then informed my superior, I did not make any mistakes. My superior officer never handed me any assignments saying that I should take my first detachment on a mission, or my second detachment, or setting out exactly how I should do something. He would tell me what I was supposed to do, and once I got this done, everything was fine. I'm not sure if you get my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Captain Karanfilov had the same rank as you. He was not in any way senior, he was a security clerk, and he was not from your own brigade command, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under all the rules, we know -- The answer was misrecorded. On page 6, line 23, the witness said "yes." Tell me, am I wrong if I say that if we look at all the rules, he had no authority to issue that order to withdraw on the 20th of November, withdraw from the hangar at Ovcara? Would I be wrong in stating that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are far wrong, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that you should not have left the hangar, based on Karanfilov's orders, before informing Vojnovic and asking and requesting his approval because he was the officer who had issued the order on that day for your company to be sent to Ovcara in the first place. Is that an erroneous conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now, but I did not know at the time that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was the one who had issued that particular assignment. If I consider that Karanfilov was introduced to me as the person in charge of a number of things there - I didn't know exactly what his position was at the time - I was certainly bound to obey Karanfilov's orders, even if he had had the rank of lieutenant-colonel, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to my learned friend Mr. Vasic's question. On the 9th of May he asked you whether perhaps you informed Dragi Vukosavljevic upon your return to Negoslavci about what had occurred. Your answer literally was: "Dragi Vukosavljevic, as far as I know but I don't remember exactly, was there." I didn't understand your answer. What do you mean by "there"; Negoslavci or Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember which soldiers and which officers exactly were at Ovcara on the 20th. I said this: When I returned I passed by command. I'm not sure exactly who I met there or who I spoke to. My answer yesterday was in reference to the fact that I found out that Dragi, too, had been at Ovcara. So he knew the same thing that I did. He knew as much as I did. Some people even told me that he was the one who had told me that I should withdraw with my military police unit, but I don't quite remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will base my questions on these facts precisely, something that I read in your previous statements. What would you say if I told you that the withdrawal order had been handed to you by Captain First Class Dragi Vukosavljevic who was chief of security of the 80th Brigade? Do you think that is possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the first time that someone has suggested this to me. This is not the first time I hear it. It wasn't only you who suggested it, that's what I'm trying to say. This is not the first time I've heard this assumption. Again, I don't remember that particular detail. I don't remember him telling me this. I withdrew my company pursuant to Captain Karanfilov's orders, which is not to say that Captain Dragi may not, in fact, have said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "the same thing"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just suggested, for the military police company to withdraw. The simple fact is, I personally do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now please go to a portion of your testimony in the Belgrade trial, the 29th of October, 2004, page 66 of the transcript. The English reference is page 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the Chamber please instruct me on this. I do not wish to go long on this one. Because the OTP may not like it. I will confront the witness with an answer which includes the question posed by a judge incorporating the words of another witness. Under our rules here, the rules governing our work, this is perfectly fine. I'm not sure if I should just read the answer or both the question and answer. I have highlighted the relevant portions for the benefit of the Chamber, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before my learned friend does so, could I just locate exactly what he's going to put to see if I do have any objections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 66 in the B/C/S and 65 in the English. The question is -- well, there is mention of a name there, I'm not supposed to utter it. This is the Presiding Judge. At line 15 you see there is the mention of someone else's evidence, the evidence of another witness. You realise that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question to the Chamber is, can I read out to the witness both the question and the answer, just to set things into the right kind of perspective?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that particular question being formulated the way my learned friend is intending. He's perfectly entitled to ask the question in generality, but he would not, in my submission, be entitled to rely upon apparent evidence of an individual who has not given evidence before this Court. There are ways around it, I would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My problem at the moment is that I have a page which has many questions and I don't know which one we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's highlighted in your copy. This is the second passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Highlighted in my copy is about two-thirds of the page. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question and an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Before I read to the witness the answer, can I read the question too? I was expecting what Mr. Moore just said. There is someone else's evidence being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I need to read it for the first time. It seems to me, Mr. Lukic, that there are a number of propositions there that are put to this witness by, it appears, the Presiding Judge. There's not just one issue. It would be proper for you, I would suggest, to go through the ones you think are important, and at least in the first place pose them to the witness yourself. You've done part of that, as I recall your cross-examination in the last few minutes, but perhaps you've not done all of it. And judging on those answers, if you get an answer, for example, that he was told by Karanfilov to withdraw - I'm giving you an illustration now, it is not necessarily reflected here - you can put to him, Have you said at the court in so and so, that it wasn't Karanfilov, right? Now I know that is not what is here. I'm searching for things to try to assist you the way you go about it. And if he then says, No, I didn't say that in the court, you can show him the particular answer here where it's recorded that he did say it, rather than put the whole passage to him. Now, that process will need to be repeated for, I suspect, two or three propositions at least, out of this full passage. Is that clear enough? That, I take it, meets your concern as well, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope Your Honour doesn't think me awkward in any way, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I think doesn't greatly matter, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully submit that my learned friend Mr. Lukic can pose the question in a way that does not involve names and with regard to a proposition what occurred. For example, "Is it not right that you are aware that another witness has said X and Y?" And he can give a reply to that. He doesn't have to give the name of the witness. And if it is done that way, I would submit he can deal with the topic absolutely on point, it expands the area, if need be, and I would submit -- and I in no way criticise Your Honour, because Your Honour is the ruling Judge, but it is -- almost concerns the whole page and it's being taken in isolation and I'm sure my learned friend doesn't wish that to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are addressing a part of this process that I was not specifically addressing. I'm first of all concerned to get the basic propositions that are in here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- identified. If we then come to a question, Well, are you aware that your evidence is quite different from evidence of other witnesses, that can be dealt with as an issue as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By the end of it, it may become feasible and practical and proper to put the whole passage to the witness, but not until we see how these earlier stages go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukic, you've had coaching from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being coached all the time, and that is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, you have been asked various questions in various proceedings, and you claim that the order on withdrawal from the hangar was given to you by Karanfilov. You were asked in various proceedings whether it is possible that the same order was issued to you but by Dragi Vukosavljevic. You said you didn't remember but that it was possible that he said that. Would that be the gist of all the questions and all the answers about that fact so far?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may answer just briefly, the order and my execution involving Captain Karanfilov, that is the fact, and the second part is based on the fact that I had learned that. I don't remember, but I did hear that somebody else had heard that, or had seen it. But I don't remember. I myself do not recall that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Somebody else heard and saw Dragi Vukosavljevic issuing that order to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am not going to confront you with the transcript that was the question, but I have to ask you this: A few days ago in your testimony you remembered some of the details when somebody prompted you. To be more specific, you answered to the Prosecutor that Novica Trifunovic told you that on that day you had gone to Nijemci and then in a conversation with him you remembered all the details; that you went to Nijemci, that he went with you, and that you carried money for the troops. Novica Trifunovic refreshed your memory in that sense; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't just give you a yes or a no. I have to say that the details of that journey and the money that was taken there, only a couple of us were privy to that, and if he was one of those few people, then of course he remembers and I accepted that. I could not remember the exact date when we did that. He remembered the date and I accepted that, so this is all I agreed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Novica Trifunovic reminded you of that journey to Nijemci, did he also remind you that he was standing in front of the hangar when Dragi Vukosavljevic conveyed the order to you? Did you also remember that, that is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have already answered that. I do not remember that conversation between myself and Dragi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am not going to confront you with a long transcript, in order to avoid any objections by my learned friend. I'm just going to read to you what you stated on page 69, and the English version page 68, and this is towards the top of the page -- the bottom of the page, some 10 lines before the end of the page: "Witness Dragi Vezmarovic: When I received the order to withdraw the troops, I withdrew the troops, and this was enough. And this was in keeping what I had been told. "The Presiding Judge: Very well then. "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: "From the person who could have issued that order; i.e., the person who was in that position, and I'm not excluding the possibility that this was said to me by Dragi, Karanfilov that both of them told me this." When you said "Dragi," you are referring to Dragi Vukosavljevic, but this is not in the transcript. And I'm asking you again, based on what you said then, a year and a half ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm sorry, this is a -- I'm afraid a deliberate misshaping of the evidence given. I regret to have to say that, but it is quite clearly that. My learned friend has not referred to other answers given, in English, page 65, when in actual fact Vezmarovic gives a very specific reply, saying, "That's right, that's right." He refers to "the same thing." Again, that has not been done. My learned friend, Mr. Lukic, has again, I regret to say, clearly deliberately not continued with the reply given on page 69, because there is a question by the judge: "What was Captain Karanfilov's exact order?" Answer: "To withdraw." The witness in this transcript has said that there was the possibility that Dragi gave the same order, but he has not deviated in any way from the fact that it was Karanfilov who gave a specific order to him. My learned friend is shaping his questions in a way to try and mislead this witness. It is unfair and improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would not, in the circumstances, agree, Mr. Moore, that there was any such objective apparent. Mr. Lukic has been trying to be careful to comply with the guidance he might receive from this Chamber. And I think, if this issue is explored a little further, the substance of the point will properly emerge. If it doesn't, the Chamber will ensure it does. No need for that comment. Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, let me go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have read out the transcript to you, what you stated before the trial chamber in Belgrade. Do you still adhere by what you said in Belgrade, and that is that you do not exclude the possibility that the order was also conveyed to you by your chief of security and that this was the order of the commander? In other words, that the order to withdraw from the hangar was conveyed to you by Dragi Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and answer that. I heard a lot of things as being facts, and I'm not escaping facts. If somebody claims that they were with me, I will accept that, although I do not remember any such thing. If somebody says that they told me that, or that they heard somebody else telling me that, I will accept that as a fact, but this is not what I recall and what I know. Within that context, I gave this answer. I accepted the fact that somebody had heard something and that such a possibility existed. But at the same time, I did not say that I remember things and that I acted according to that. I don't know whether I have managed to answer your question. Not for a single moment in Belgrade or here have I remembered having received such an instruction. However, if a number of people claim that they heard and that they are aware of that, I cannot say that this is not a fact, that this is not true. I can't remember, but if I accept that as being the truth, and they asked me the same thing there, and the question was whether there is a possibility that I had received such an order from Dragi, if five people say that that was a fact, I cannot escape from that fact, but I myself do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question about the facts: Do you remember that in front of the hangar on that day there was a soldier, Soldier Novica Trifunovic, who returned with you to Negoslavci. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you've asked me the same thing already, and my answer was, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm repeating: If they claim that they were there and if Trifunovic says that he was in front of the door, I know that there were soldiers in front of the door, but I don't know whether he was among them. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to draw a comparison with what you have already said and that is if Trifunovic had reminded you that you were in the village of Nijemci with him, did you accept that in the same way? If he claims that that was the fact, then that must have been the fact, and you are now doing the same thing. But you do not remember either of the two.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two different things. The fact that he reminded me of the date when we were there is one thing. I do not remember all the details of our journey to Nijemci, our return from there. I can't even say that I took only the two of them from Negoslavci to Ovcara, or maybe there was somebody else with us. If I can't remember things, I can't remember them. However, the fact that we were in Nijemci is a fact, and I accepted it because I know that I was there, I know why I went, but I could not recall the date. Since he remembered the date, and he was aware of all the facts involving Nijemci, I could also agree with the date that he offered. And as to whether that soldier was there, whether he was standing on the left or on the right, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My following question is this: When Karanfilov arrived and said what he said to you, at that moment you did not address your commander Vojnovic, and you didn't ask him whether to Ovcara or not. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer with either a yes or a no. On the 19th, when I handed over to the Mitnica group, I did not address my commander. I didn't address him on the 20th either. I believe that it sufficed for me to have an officer, superior officer who is in charge of things, and I communicated with him and after the events I could only inform the commander what had happened, whether things were in order or not. And this was my line of thinking, and under the conditions, I believe that it was the correct thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this Trial Chamber you testified that Karanfilov had remained in Ovcara when you left, and you stated that on the 9th of May, transcript page 35. Are you sure of that? Are you positive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'm sure of: When my troops were ready to leave, the last thing I did, I greeted everybody. I -- I'm sure of that. At that moment, I was sitting in the car and I actually told them I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the page 61 of the Belgrade trial transcript. And in the English version I'd like to refer you to page 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first paragraph, Your Honour, that I have provided you with from the transcript that I am going to confront the witness with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Presiding Judge: You said before the investigating judge of the military court that after you had handed over the prisoners -" and he quotes you - "'Together with my troops in three Pinzgauers, I returned to Negoslavci and Captain Karanfilov came with me.' This is what you said before the investigating judge in the military court." Your answer to that: "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: Possibly, I really cannot remember. That he returned with me? "Presiding Judge: That he returned to Negoslavci with you. 'Captain Karanfilov came with me.' "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic --" I shall repeat page 18, line 9: Karanfilov -- "Captain Karanfilov came with me." And before that, the Presiding Judge asked you whether he returned to Negoslavci with you, your answer to that: "I cannot exclude this possibility, but I don't really remember. It is possible." "Presiding Judge: All right. Did ...?" And now your answer: "If I said that he had returned in my vehicle, this is certainly not the fact. He definitely didn't come in any of my vehicles, but maybe he joined the column in his own vehicle." This was your answer to the Presiding Judge, who confronted you with your statement given before the investigating judge. Since you said here that Karanfilov had stayed, and in 1999, in the military court you said that he had left with you, I'm asking you now, before this Trial Chamber, whether you still claim that Karanfilov had remained in Ovcara or he might have left with you, or he certainly left with you. What is your statement? What is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find my bearings in the text that you have just read out, but anyway let's try and answer. I don't think that I said anything differently to what you have just said. And I repeat: We said our good-byes and I departed. Whether Captain Karanfilov followed me or not, in his own car or not, I can't remember. And I repeat what I've already said: He did not ride in any of my vehicles because he had his own vehicle. Whether he stayed behind or not, whether he came to the command or not, I really can't remember. When I said he stayed behind, I meant to say that I don't know whether he stayed for two, three, four, five hours there. What I meant was that at the moment when I sat in the car and when I departed, he stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's why you said before the military court that he left with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to locate that. I don't know why I said that. At the moment, he was getting ready to leave, but he didn't leave with me. I really can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't see such a specific answer in the evidence that you've read out. Merely a possibility that he might have left in his own vehicle, and his own vehicle might have joined the column, that this witness was not able to say that occurred. Isn't that the effect of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was stated before the Belgrade trial chamber, however I'm going confront the witness with the statement given to the military court, the oldest statement, dating from 1999, when his recollection was the freshest. Let me just try and locate that passage. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, the first passage on the top of that page. I'm sure that you have been able to locate it, Mr. Vezmarovic. "Captain Karanfilov came with me." And you can read for yourself, however the gist of the matter is that you stated very clearly -- this is the fifth passage of the English version, page 5. Your sentence is very -- leaves no doubt when you say, "Captain Karanfilov came with me." My question to you is as follows: In 1999, was your recollection somewhat better?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recollection is recollection, and I'm repeating: At the moment when I departed, he stayed behind. It says here he came with me. He did not depart with me, if I'm reading the text well. This only means that something else was said together with that sentence. Departed and came are two different things, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am drawing my cross-examination to an end. We have talked quite a lot here, and I have two final questions for you. If you received the withdrawal order from Captain Karanfilov, do you believe that you acted in the same way as you acted two days ago when you handed the prisoners over to another unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have said that many times. From the moment I arrived to the moment when I withdrew, I did everything by the book in order to provide security for the prisoners and that, in my view and in my estimate, they were safe, that I was given an order to withdraw, and that I withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your question is -- your answer is clear. Do you believe that you acted by the book as you did two days before that, and that you respected all the rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed over the Mitnica group to Captain Karanfilov in that same way, and the second time I handed the second group to Captain Karanfilov, I did the same. The officer who was standing in front of me was the officer that I was supposed to -- I can't put it in words, but this was an officer whom I trusted, because the first job was followed through properly and I did not have a single reason that 24 hours later things had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My case, Mr. Vezmarovic, is that the order was issued to you by Mr. Vukosavljevic, but since you said that it is possible that Dragi Vukosavljevic also gave you that order, I will ask you something else. If you say that it is possible that Dragi Vukosavljevic gave you that order, do you believe that if Dragi Vukosavljevic conveyed an order to you given to him by his superior, that you acted by the book, that you the respected all the rules, if you did what you did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood you well. If Dragi Vukosavljevic issued an order to me that he had been given by the commander, whether I acted by the book. The security organ was the organ that was in the position to issue an order to me at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vezmarovic. I have no further questions and apologise for going at such a great length, but I think we have been able to demonstrate quite a lot of things to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have been of any assistance in clarifying certain facts, it has been my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now, Mr. Borovic, you have an issue that you need to take up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to clarify one particular issue remaining from yesterday, and you promised that I would be given the time to deal with that, because one of the questions and one of the answers provided by the witness hasn't been clarified sufficiently, and if I may, I would like to do that now. Thank you. First of all, I would like to ask the usher to hand over these documents to the witness. And there are copies for the Chamber as well. I've brought here the pages pertaining to those statements, so as to have a clear picture of what I will be asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we go through documents, Mr. Borovic, and I would say this for the witness. Captain. If you would stop reading the documents for a moment. It would be important if you could simply clarify from the witness's own recollection what his movements were, the basic movements on the night of the 18th, 19th of November, 1991, the day of the 19th of November, and the night of the 19th/20th of November, and his movements during the day of the 20th. That appears to be the area of confusion, and it would be very important in terms of credibility if the Chamber could hear his actual recollection about his movements on those days before you come, if you need or wish to, to test whether that recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps you are now giving me greater powers than I thought I would have today. I thought we would only deal with one question that was denied by the witness when it came to the math I did. Because there were a few hours missing that he tried to explain in a different way. But if I may be permitted, I will deal with the entire topic and things will be crystal clear. If we go and read out three things, and we've heard the witness's answers to Mr. Lukic today, should we go through such an exercise, everything would become very clear. If I may do it that way, I will be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, perhaps I might put some questions to the witness, and then if you need, you may follow on the issue that concerns you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber when it was that you first went to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic and myself were touring the area, looking for a facility that could accommodate greater numbers of detainees, and we found the hangar at Ovcara to be suitable for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand from your evidence that the decision was made to use Ovcara, and that later that day you, with others, were involved in preparing the hangar to receive prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was to find a facility, a building. Had we gone through Ovcara without finding such a building, we would have moved on elsewhere. We didn't go to Ovcara specifically to find that one building. We were just looking for a building. I hope this is sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was clear. My concern was moving on. I think a decision was made to use Ovcara to hold prisoners, and later on the 18th you were involved in preparations of the hangar at Ovcara to receive prisoners.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when prisoners first arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, sometime around 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how did they -- you were there, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had arrived a few moments before the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How did prisoners arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an organised convoy. The prisoners were on buses, and in front of the column there were military vehicles. There was a Puch and there were military vehicles at the back and at the front of the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... trying to move in summary, we're not asking for full details of all of this at the moment. Were these prisoners from Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was explained that these were the prisoners who had surrendered at Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These were Croatian military prisoners, or some other type?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They were held at Ovcara in the hangar overnight?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they remained in the hangar throughout the night and the next morning, when they were collected by the international organisations and the Red Cross, as well as the JNA, and they were supposed to be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you at Ovcara throughout that night, which is the 18th and 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Negoslavci occasionally in order to secure everything that was needed for the security detail, the food and water. But I was in the hangar most of the time. I may have left for Negoslavci on a couple of occasions for short periods of time because there were problems with supply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did only one group of prisoners arrive, or were there others that arrived later over the night of the 18th and the morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the only group that arrived, around 4.00 p.m. on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next morning you have indicated that a transport arrived to take these prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica; is that correct? And Captain Karanfilov was there when you, in your effective words, handed the prisoners over to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when the convoy arrived, that is the buses, Captain Karanfilov and myself had that dialogue. I reported on the previous night, he asked me about the list of prisoners. I told him that I had that in my notebook. He said that I should go to Negoslavci to type the list in order to have it with the transport with the prisoners, and I did so. When I said that I told -- that I handed the prisoners over to him, I meant to say that after that I was no longer at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see the convoy leave with the prisoners that morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had left before the prisoners were put on buses. I wasn't present at that moment, and I wasn't within the escort of the convoy when they departed for Sremska Mitrovica, because that was the time when I was typing out the list. I don't know exactly what time they set out, who escorted the convoy, how large was it, and how secure was it. At that time, I was typing the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your evidence is that the list was typed, the convoy had already left by then, and you were ordered to follow the convoy to Sremska Mitrovica with the list of the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not to follow, but I attempted to reach Mitrovica or to -- I failed to catch up with the convoy, and at the time when I actually delivered the list was in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The prisoners were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the prisoners in Mitrovica, but I was told that they had arrived and were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To whom did you hand the list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact name. Judging by what I wrote down in my notebook, those must have been some officers that I gave the list to. It must have been one of the officers at the prison. The list included the number of people they received, and the number matched the number on the list, and that was all right then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was 175 soldiers and six officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you estimate what time it was when you delivered the list at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my entries, I presume it was around 4.00 or 4.30 p.m., otherwise I can't be exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I returned to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate what time you reached Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It already got dark. I tried to do the calculation that was attempted here as well, and I believe by the time I arrived there it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nightfall is before 5.00 p.m., is it? Mid-November.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. Depending on what the weather was that day. But trying to remember, I was trying to pin-point the things that I did along the way. So my assumption was that I reached Negoslavci at around 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say that's an assumption. The journey itself would have taken a lot less time than that if you'd travelled directly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, as I said, as of the moment I concluded my business at the prison, I didn't go to Negoslavci directly, but I stopped along the way. That's why I presume it took me such a long time, judging by the stops I made and the things I did there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you outline quickly what these other things were that you did between Sremska Mitrovica and Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left the prison, but the driver and myself stayed for a while in Mitrovica. I don't know how long, though, but we rented out a room, we took showers, we had dinner there, and then we set off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you make any stops on the way, once you'd left Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coming in any village or leaving the village, there were always patrols, and that's why things took longer and it had already gotten dark by that time. So the entire procedure lasted longer than it would have at day-time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Apart from patrol stops, did you stop for any purpose of your own on the way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You arrived at Negoslavci. Did you go to your headquarters or any other headquarters on arrival?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the command, I reported to someone, but I don't exactly remember who. I told that person that I had delivered the list, that things were fine, and then I went to my own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went about my routine tasks. During the night there was an intervention concerning an incident in one of the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying you were on duty through that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of that night. Before morning I did have some time to take a rest, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the particular incident that took you away from Negoslavci on the night, now, of the 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, there was a murder of a soldier, and we were called in to secure the site until the other bodies showed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, near Sotin somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you yourself were at Sotin for a time, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you left Sotin, are you able to say where you went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you estimate when you arrived at your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably around midnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was resting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: After you had rested, what did you do then? And I take it we're now in the morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Routine tasks on the 20th, up until the moment when we needed to provide a car, a vehicle to take the people who were supposed to distribute the salaries to pick up the money and distribute it. Then we took a Pinzgauer, there was the driver, myself, and the people who were supposed to distribute the money. There may have been both Novica and Sapic as well. I can accept that proposition put to me here. I don't remember what exactly had been said, but in any case, we set off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did you set off to escort the salaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 11.00 and 12.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you return to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I understand that you asked me whether I returned to my command, to my headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we concluded with the task, I returned to my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And what time was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark as well, but I can't guess at what time it was. I don't remember the exact time, but it was dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you returned directly to your headquarters after completing the salaries escort duty; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trip included a double task for me. First of all, we had to secure the people who were supposed to distribute the salaries. The other thing was that I tried to familiarise myself with the terrain there, in case I would have to send out a patrol for any reason, to be able to explain to the driver how to go there. It was a way for me to familiarise myself with the area, as I had no map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which area was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, when we were going to Nijemci we had to go through Sid, and then all the way almost up to the highway, and then on a side road to reach Nijemci. In the end, we spent a lot of time waiting for the minesweeper. They had to perform their task because that was the only safe way to reach Nijemci at the moment. One of the officers who was with us stayed behind in one of the villages where our soldiers were. He distributed the salaries there, and at the same time the rest of us went as far as Nijemci and the person distributed money there, and then we went back. When we reached individual units, it didn't necessarily have to be that they would get off the -- or out of the vehicle to distribute the money, but they would simply give the money and then we would leave again. We were all reservists, we knew each other, we had short discussions, and we would stay a while at every place, a short while, and then we would move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you returned to your headquarters after dark on the 20th of November, what occurred then at your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer reported that the company was securing Ovcara and that there was a new group of prisoners who had to be secured. Together with the soldiers who were available and off duty, I took a vehicle and we went to Ovcara. On our way we stopped by at the command, but I don't remember whom I met there and what I was told as I wanted to get together with my unit as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What time was it that you reached Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It was dark, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, at Ovcara you have described how you found a considerable degree of disorder, and you set about, you have indicated, establishing order, initially by ensuring that all left the hangar except men of your military police unit and the prisoners. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did that include officers and soldiers who were required to leave the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not officers. Those who had rank did not pose problems. The problem I had was to distinguish between the soldiers there. And I didn't know whether the soldiers were from the 80th Brigade or not, that's why I said that everyone except for those with the white belts had to leave. Therefore, officers were no problem specifically. As to which of the officers was there and whether they left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did that include territorial officers as well as JNA officers who remained in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for TO officers, I did my best to get in touch with them. I asked them to come forward, to respond, but no one did. No one came forward to say that they were TO officers. Therefore, I don't really know whether any of them were there. But what I was able to infer at the time later proved to have been true. There were two of them, but they didn't speak up. They commanded with their eyes, in a manner of speaking, and they all eventually left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So there were no territorial officers left inside the hangar once it was cleared of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say all of this occurred after dark; your return to Negoslavci, to your headquarters, and then your journey to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you give any approximation of time, either for your arrival at Negoslavci or for your arrival at Ovcara on the evening of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't specify the time of my arrival in Negoslavci or at Ovcara. But my rough estimate would be that I stayed for between one and a half and two hours at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, Mr. Borovic, I have done that, unusually, to clear up a number of matters, including setting the framework for you then to decide what you need to explore or not. But in doing so I have used up the time to the first break. Your microphone, Mr. Borovic, could you turn it off? Thank you. Then we won't get the feedback. I've used up the time to the first break, which we must have now for the tapes. But that will enable you then to set your sights on what you need to do. And we will then resume at 25 past 11.00 for the evidence to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the distance between Negoslavci and Nijemci in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Negoslavci and Nijemci, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You will have to do your best to remember. You were the one who travelled that road. Please be so kind. I think the distance is probably the same now as it was back then. So what would that be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What if I tell you that it is under 30 kilometres; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is my estimate accurate, given the fact that you travelled the road in a vehicle, the road between Negoslavci and Nijemci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in terms of kilometres? Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did it take for you to cover those 30 kilometres? Taking into account all the difficulty that you encountered along the way, as you told the Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again the answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would it have been sufficient for you, say up to an hour, to cover that distance, in a car? Or could it possibly have taken less time than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did a bit of calculating the last time around, and when I gave evidence I tried to do my own math, what the distance was and how long it would have taken, but whatever further calculations we engage in will only be speculation and no more than that. You have a distance of 30 kilometres. Driving and traffic conditions being what they were in the area at the time, so these being the parameters, I would say under an hour, yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us proceed. It would have taken you roughly the same amount of time to drive back, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we want to just round it off, in that case, I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said in answer to the Chamber's question today that you had left a soldier behind in Negoslavci, and you yourself drove back to Nijemci. My question: Does that mean you returned at about 2.00 p.m.? Returned to Negoslavci, I mean. Because that is the math we're talking about. This is your contribution to this Tribunal, this is what your evidence is suppose to contribute, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, please show us the way. Let us in on this secret. We did some math, and we arrived at a figure of two hours, whereas you suggest nine hours. Between noon and half past 8.00 in the evening, that's nearly nine hours. Did you take nine hours to cover those 30 kilometres? You were pretty particular when answering a question posed by the Chamber. You left a soldier behind in Nijemci and you drove back to Negoslavci. So is it two hours or nine hours to drive back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hours is certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which is the maximum that you would allow for your return for the 30-kilometre distance on the way back? Sir, let me explain why I'm pursuing this issue. You remember those hotel rooms, you remember taking showers during wartime, you remember all these tiny details that you would not have remembered before the war. All these details are essential to us, and you keep telling us you don't remember. Please be so kind as to at least try to specify this: Could it have been a maximum of three hours, up to three hours for you to cover that distance, the distance between Negoslavci and Nijemci, and then back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there are possibly two or three questions there. I will tackle one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, there is no such thing as two or three questions there. There is just one single question. Whenever you don't have an answer, you start saying things like there are several questions in there. How much time did it take you to drive from Negoslavci to Nijemci and back? A total of how long, since I see that your memory is a bit fresher today.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at about noon, probably between 11.00 and 12.00 a.m., that's when I left. And by the time I arrived it was already dark. I believe that's what I said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A total of how many hours? You remember you left between 11.00 and 12.00. That is pretty accurate, if you ask me. When you say it was already dark, it could have been 4.30 in the afternoon, as the Presiding Judge suggested. It was already dark. That might as well be a useful excuse for you not to say. Please try to specify how long it took you to cover that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to the tone of my learned friend's questions. I don't mind questions being asked on the topic but it's really not proper for him to put in comments, his views on what the witness may or may not be saying by way of excuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, Mr. Borovic. But please press home your point, as you are. I meant the fair comment was Mr. Moore's. Your comments are not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I accept the criticism. I will try to proceed more subtly with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said you left between 11.00 and 12.00, you left for Nijemci, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said you don't know when exactly it was that your company left for Ovcara on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you allow for the possibility that your company left for Ovcara past 12.00, past noon, any time after 12.00?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that they arrived at Ovcara the same time as the prisoners, when they arrived outside the hangar? Do you allow for that possibility that at the time the prisoners arrived, your company was there as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, if my learned friend is asking the question in relation to this witness's personal knowledge, that question is perfectly fair. If it's in relation to another aspect of his company, he is asking the witness to speculate. Could he perhaps be clearer in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the facts are clear, Mr. Borovic. The witness says he was away from between 11.00 and 12.00. He doesn't know what the men left behind did. When he got back to his headquarters, he was told they were at Ovcara. So he can't really fill in what they did in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does the witness know if there is a phone line between the village of Negoslavci and the village of Nijemci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the witness perhaps remember this: Does the witness remember being called by Commander Vojnovic to go back to Negoslavci urgently because there was a job at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the possibility exists that Commander Vojnovic called you to drive back from Negoslavci urgently because there was a job to be done at Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: -- since you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness is being asked to speculate again. The answer is quite simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's enough for your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Enough for your purposes simply to have the basic facts. You want to get the witness to agree to an inference from those facts, which is beyond his knowledge, and that's a matter for us to assess at the end of all of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As always, you are right yet again. I didn't mean to lead the witness. Had he said in a determined manner he didn't call, that would have been fine. But he said, "I don't remember." Well, I will just press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The witness states that at the Ovcara trial in Belgrade on the 29th of October, 2004, he spoke to Novica Trifunovic after the session and Novica Trifunovic jogged his memory about Nijemci.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Back in 2004.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea when that was, but it was during the actual trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day you both gave evidence before the trial chamber in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact day, but you must have checked the date, and that should be it, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I gave you copies of those statements. They appear to have been taken away from you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you must have checked the date yourself, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I think it is for you to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is crucial, Your Honours. I must show the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement to the OTP in front of you, number 1? Tab 1, it's marked as tab 1. Do you have that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: International Criminal Tribunal, witness statement, personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You do have the statement in front of you, don't you, the 2001 statement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2001, Belgrade, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you the statement that you gave on the 29th of October, 2004, in the Belgrade Ovcara case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it that day -- so was it on that day that you talked to Novica Trifunovic? Was this the trial you referred to, the 29th of October, 2004, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. If Novica was there on the same day, then that should be it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please check the transcript and see if Novica Trifunovic was there on the same day. If you just go through it quickly, you will see his name being mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does that mean that you never spoke with Novica Trifunovic about Nijemci after this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement on the 17th of October, 2005? Yes or no. Did you give a statement on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't seem to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You testified with Novica Trifunovic at the Belgrade trial on the 29th of October, 2004, which you have just confirmed. A year later did you again give evidence before a court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give evidence, but I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have it right there in front of you, the transcript bears the date the 17th of October, 2005.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So that was a year after the one you gave in 2004.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I have an unofficial English translation. I'm not sure if the Chamber has it, I think the OTP does. But without necessarily driving the point home, you don't mention Nijemci at all. Again you talk about Negoslavci, you talk about going to Ovcara in the afternoon. I won't be quoting the statement now, but my general question is, is it now that you've arrived in The Hague that you have suddenly remembered everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before my learned friend asks the question, we don't have any statement, we have not had anything served on us, we don't have any translation of it. I'd be awfully grateful if my learned friends could perhaps pass it to us. I'm sure it's our fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help me, Mr. Borovic. This is a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a transcript, and then there is tab 3, what I had marked as tab 3, page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... transcript of evidence given at a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 17th, the 17th. My apologies, Your Honours. There's been an overlap. This is the transcript of this witness's evidence on the 17th of October, 2005, which he just confirmed a minute ago. This was a year after his conversation with Novica Trifunovic back in 2004, who apparently jogged his memory about Nijemci. Here we have the Presiding Judge asking a question, and there is a couple of answers. I can read this and the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: "Dragan Vezmarovic: Yes. The morning of the day after I received an assignment from Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic to catch up with the convoy before Mitrovica or perhaps in Mitrovica, if I don't manage before, and to hand over the list of prisoners, so I was on my way to Mitrovica. In Mitrovica I handed over the list to the officers of the prison, who were already there. I don't know their names. I then returned to Negoslavci sometime in the afternoon or late in the afternoon or early in the evening. We were in that house where the unit was billeted." And this is what really matters, this part: "I learned from the duty officer that we had another security group at that same place. And it was then that I again drove to Ovcara." Later on, the Presiding Judge asks him about the time-line and the witness says he can't be specific about that, but that the relevant notes should be somewhere in his notebook. Mr. Vezmarovic, have you got that? This is page 5. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 33, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was my reading accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the other one that you have in front of you? You appear to be claiming there that you don't know what the time was when you arrived at Ovcara, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We agree on that. My question is a very clear-cut one. A year ago you say that you found out from a soldier about Nijemci, something which you seem to go into a lot of detail about in your evidence to this Tribunal. Why did you not mention that at the Ovcara trial in Belgrade back in 2005? Is there any explanation that you can offer for that circumstance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were reading and I was trying to keep track. Perhaps you can give me a hand with this. If I'm not mistaken, at the end of the dialogue between the Presiding Judge and myself, the judge told me that this was about a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you find that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There is no reason.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at this point the Presiding Judge told me that there was a one-day discrepancy, and then I tried to look into this matter to figure it out. I'm sure you know what I mean. Both then and on earlier occasions I always repeated the same thing: I don't remember the time, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're quite right there, you didn't know at the time. But it is right here, right now, that you have talked about Nijemci for the very first time. I have been following very closely. Both on examination-in-chief and in cross-examination you were quite specific. You found out from your own soldier at this trial in 2004, October, 2004, about this. On the 17th of October, 2005, you say nothing about it. How am I supposed to believe you when you say that your memory was jogged by Novica Trifunovic, your own soldier, back in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had you been listening to me, had you remembered exactly what I had been saying, you would know. I'm telling you it was the Presiding Judge who put this to me about this one-day discrepancy. I did say that a couple of minutes ago, and then I tried to figure it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what did you do afterwards, what did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you seconds ago that I didn't talk to Novica then, not alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Dear, sir, I'm about to finish my cross-examination with the distinct impression that you are trying to dodge this particular issue. Novica Trifunovic told you back in 2004, the Presiding Judge reminded you again. You stand by your old story. My distinct impression is you got this impression during your proofing sessions in preparation for your testimony before this Chamber and this Tribunal. I can only state the fact, but I do not wish to go any further or wreck anyone's nerves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes my cross-examination, Your Honours, and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, may we just deal with the transcript that was placed before you, or certainly read to you for the hearing of the 17th of October, 2005. Has that been provided to you?
