On the English version that we now have, it's page 5 of 33. Now, do you have that document? 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And on the English it's page 5/33, and it's really an exchange between the Presiding Judge and yourself. And there is a series of three questions. Now, it starts off, I hope: "So, in the morning the day after?" Have you got that or not? And I would like you to be very precise, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text, but I'm not sure which passage you are referring to on page 5. What exactly should I be looking at? I have the Serbian. That's it, it's the same thing. All right. Just give me the passage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Okay. I will give you the two lead-in lines, if I may. The first lead-in line is the Presiding Judge is asking the following question: "So, in the morning the day after?" And then we've got your name as the witness, and it starts: "Yes, in the morning the day after ..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want you to listen very carefully, please, to what I'm going to ask you to do. I want you to read out this question and answer, slowly and accurately, please, so that we get the full context of the way the question and answer proceeded. Now, can you do that, or shall I do it for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, but my copy is in Serbian. "Presiding Judge: So, the morning of the day after? "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: Yes, the morning of day after, it was then that I received an assignment from Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic to catch up with the convoy to Mitrovica, or perhaps in Mitrovica, and if I didn't manage to catch up, I was supposed to hand over the list of prisoners, - so I was off to Mitrovica with the driver. Once in Mitrovica, I handed over the list to prison officers who were already there, - I don't know their exact names, I then returned to Negoslavci, sometime that afternoon or early evening. The place where we were billeted, the house where the unit was, I learned from the duty officer that we had another security group right there. I then again went to Ovcara to see what this was all about. Should I proceed and tell you what was going on?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge says: "Yes, yes." Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: All right. What I found there was quite a mess. There were prisoners in the hangar itself, therefore, in the same building as before, were not being guarded as they had been the previous day, meaning they were not in one part of the hangar being guarded by the military police, but rather they were assembled in groups inside the hangar itself. I ordered everyone to leave. In addition to military police company members, there were other people, all kinds of people in all kinds of uniforms inside the hangar. I ordered everyone to leave the hangar except the police and prisoners. After a while, everyone had left the hangar and all prisoners were again sent to the same corner of the building where they had been the day before. A rope was strung up again in order to draw a line of separation and divide the prisoners from the rest. The military police were on the job again, both inside and outside the hangar. While I was ordering everyone to leave the hangar, I promised everyone who was there that I would let them have a look later on and perhaps identify some of the prisoners. So I allowed this later on. They walked around the rope, identified or failed to identify people, and made comments all the while, both inside and outside the hangar. About the people they had seen in there and who it was that they had seen. After a while, Captain Karanfilov ordered me to withdraw the company, to withdraw the policemen who were there, since an agreement had been reached that these would now be handed over to Vukovar's TO units. Therefore, I assembled all of the policemen who were there, we got back into the Pinzgauer, and went back to Negoslavci. That's about it. "Presiding Judge: And when did you return?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you do it more slowly, please, because the interpreters have to travel rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Presiding Judge: And when did you return? "Witness Vezmarovic: "Well, I can only say that it was sometime in the afternoon when I departed from Mitrovica. I arrived in Negoslavci at a certain time, and from Negoslavci I went to Ovcara. I spent some time there and I'm sure that it was dark. Now, what the time it was really, I can't remember either the date or the time. Those meant nothing to me. We were there on an assignment, we were there to do something, to accomplish something, so I never cared about the time or the date. I even didn't make a note of that in my notebook. This is my mistake, but that's the way it was. "Presiding Judge: Very well, then. Can we now --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think we're going move on to another topic. I just want to deal with that, can you just stop for a moment? It's been suggested to you by my learned friend Mr. Borovic that really you are, putting it politely, fabricating your evidence and changing your evidence here at court. Now, can you explain why there is a difference with regard to the route, as has been suggested to you by Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, while I was looking at the pages I found the passage that can answer your question, and if you will allow me, I can read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it is. I wish somebody would stop switching off my mic. But I have no objection to you doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not interrupted the witness who was reading the context that was not the subject of what I tried to establish during my cross-examination. And now the entire transcript can only refer to what the Prosecutor has to ask the witness very specifically. If now the Prosecutor asks questions about things that I never asked the witness, I believe that he hasn't the right to do that. When I questioned the witness, I asked him whether he ever said to the Presiding Judge in 2005 whether he ever mentioned Nijemci. If that is what he wants to read out, if that is something he wants to answer, I agree. If that is not the case, then I object to whatever the witness may want to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you put in too confined a way the scope of re-examination that is open to Mr. Moore. If you have opened up a topic in your cross-examination, or if you've put to the witness a proposition, that may be explored by Mr. Moore in re-examination to get another view of that matter. As I understand your cross-examination, one of the propositions you put is that effectively the witness's evidence is quite a fabrication about the dates and, as it were, the missing day. I would see that as allowing to Mr. Moore proper scope to explore how it is that there is, in part of his evidence, an unexplained day, and how it is that that unexplained day came to be identified, if it was, in any of these previous trials or hearings. So that explanation can be pursued, and I think that's what Mr. Moore is doing, and he is, with his usual fairness, allowing the witness to go to something that even Mr. Moore doesn't know where it will lead, because the witness says this is where I know I put this matter earlier. So that's open to Mr. Moore. And of course in this re-examination Mr. Moore is exploring not only your cross-examination, but also that of Mr. Lukic and Mr. Vasic. So we mustn't see it just in the light of what you've looked at. Now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, would you mind opening Pandora's box and telling us what it is that is actually said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the sentences that I exchanged with the Presiding Judge might serve as an explanation. I had a dilemma even then as to what the date was and when things happened. Not for a single moment was I certain what happened when. I saw something on one of the pages and I hope that this will help resolve the matter. The Presiding Judge explained something that I confirmed, and then the Presiding Judge says, as for the Mitnica group -- this is page 11. Page 11, somewhere in the middle it starts. "As for the Mitnica group, Colonel Karaula was the one who had a knife. This took place on the 18th, i.e., on the 17th, between the 17th and the 18th. In the morning of the 18th, they departed for Mitrovica." I will proceed reading, with a comment, if I may. If I had received information that this had happened between the 17th and the 18th, and after that something else happened on a different date, I have to repeat that if somebody tells me something, I will accept, but I do not remember myself. I am proceeding with reading my own testimony: "I believe that all this happened between the 18th and the 19th. "The Presiding Judge: So this happened in the night between the 17th and the 18th, that's where -- when they spent the night there, and what you're telling us today is one day later, on the 19th, between the 19th and the 20th, that is. If you had left on the 18th in the morning to Mitrovica, you did not return on the 19th in the evening. But on the 18th, and there is a discrepancy, a one-day discrepancy there." Again if I may comment on this, again there is confusion with the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This means -- "Presiding Judge: According to the operative log -- "Witness Vezmarovic: It says that Vukovar fell on the 17th. "Is that correct?" Answer -- Presiding Judge, yes. "Vezmarovic: If Vukovar fell on the 17th, that means that everything happened with the Mitnica group. "The Presiding Judge: This is not important at the moment. At the moment this is not important. It is not important whether this happened on the 17th, the 18th, the 19th or the 20th. The only thing that matters is the sequence of all these events. "Witness Vezmarovic: What I am trying to say -- "Presiding Judge: In your today's testimony, there is one day missing, i.e., there is a discrepancy between what we have based on the tactical operative log. "Witness Vezmarovic: At the moment when Vukovar fell, at that moment the group from Mitnica arrived, they spent the night there, and on the following day they went to Mitrovica." I did not have the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please read the following three sentences just for the fairness of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Presiding Judge: In the evening it was on the following day, based on the operative log, that that group -- in the log it says 1630, the commander issued an order to reinforce security for the camp in Ovcara. So some of the members of the command went up there, and at 2230 hours the commander issued an order for the security to be withdrawn from Ovcara. And this is what is important, and this is what Karanfilov conveyed to you, as you say." Can I go on reading until the end? "So there is a record of everything, and the times when things happened but there is one day that is missing that is at stake here."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, set aside dates, if you would kind enough, please, and I'd like you to focus on events. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you went to Ovcara in relation to the Mitnica group.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us about handing the prisoners over to Karanfilov. I want to deal, if I may, please, with the second time that you went to Ovcara. The second day, whatever date. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, if we deal with this second trip to Ovcara where you have told us -- you used the word "mayhem." Do you have, as you would perceive it, a good recollection of what occurred that afternoon and evening at the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said many times there was mayhem there. I managed to put security in order. Who was there and how long all this lasted, I really can't remember. But I managed to establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to establish order, I managed to bring order to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you specifically about your recollection of events. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I don't want to -- you to give any evidence about what you've been told by anyone. I just want you to give this Court of what you actually remember from that evening. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... want to ask any questions about possibilities, I want you to deal specifically with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who gave you the order to withdraw from Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Captain Karanfilov's order for me to withdraw, and I carried the order out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, please listen to the question very carefully. You have been told about what other people have told you. Now, have you any recollection or do you remember seeing Vukosavljevic that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so, when it comes to the -- what has been described as the possibility, you accepting the possibility of him giving you such an order, is that because of what you have been told by others of what they say they saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, what people told me and what fits in the whole picture is something that I will gladly accept as the truth. But this does not arise from my own recollection. This is based on what other people told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to deal with the cross-examination of Mr. Lukic. You have been referred to passages in the transcript when you gave evidence on the 29th of October. Now, I am afraid I cannot give my learned friends the B/C/S page number because I can't speak B/C/S, and I apologise for that, but the English version, it is page 65, and it starts off with the Presiding Judge asking you a question which commences in the following way --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can locate -- perhaps my learned friends who are bilingual and perhaps even trilingual might be able to help. The question is: "Mr. Vezmarovic, I know I asked you in which car Karanfilov had come. It is because during the investigation at the military court you said this: 'Captain Karanfilov arrived at Ovcara with his escorts in a Puch and told me that Vukovar was now fully under the command of the organs of the authority in Vukovar, the Vukovar Territorial Defence unit, and consequently these prisoners as well who have been put in the hangar in the meantime.'" . That is the passage that I wish to deal with, please. Have you got that passage or not? Or can my learned friends assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] B/C/S version page 65, towards the end of that page. This is what our learned friend has just read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we move down, we have got "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic," and you see the phrase: "It's possible, it's possible." Have you got that or not? It's important you tell us if you have or have not got that passage.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good. Perhaps if I read it and we can deal with it that way. "Presiding Judge: All right. Witness Novica Trifunovic said he talked to you in front of the hangar, in front of it. He also said that the two of them, he and Sapic, stood at the hangar door, by your orders, following your order to stand at the door and make sure that nobody entered the hangar, and that you and Captain Dragi were talking in front of the hangar and Vukoslavljevic [sic], that is, that Captain Dragi, told you to withdraw, to end the guarding, and that you were talking to him and arguing about this." Answer by yourself -- my learned friend Mr. Lukic objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the cross-examination, according to your instruction, I did not want to read the paragraph quoting, and the judge mentioning another witness, because my learned friend Moore objected to that, and now my learned friend is doing just that, quoting the judge mentioning another witness's name. I don't object to that, but your initial instruction was different and I was prevented from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reason that I mentioned the name is because the name Trifunovic was mentioned by my learned friend in -- I'm sorry, we can find the transcript of it. The name has been mentioned in cross-examination by the Defence during their cross-examination. So how on earth can my learned friend object when in actual fact -- well, we can check the transcript, it's very simple. How can my learned friend object if in actual fact the name has been mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic's recollection and position is quite correct, Mr. Moore. Now, can you tell me what it is that you are exploring with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I would submit that my learned friend Mr. Lukic was cherry-picking. I use that word in a nice phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we leave that aside. What is it that you are exploring?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am submitting that the whole reply should go before the Court so the Court can see the way this witness gave the evidence. Not only here, dealing with the topic, but also at page 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, which is the whole reply that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour has the copy. If one looks at the top, it starts: "Presiding Judge: Mr. Vezmarovic." And then it's approximately 12 lines from the bottom, where it is: "Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: That's right, that's right. But, as I was saying, I am not ruling out the possibility that I also heard Dragi say the same thing." So it's to that passage that I would submit is important, because we would be submitting the way it was put to the witness is that really there was inequivalence, whereas here what the witness is saying is that Karanfilov ordered him, and he accepts the possibility because of what others have said, that Dragi may have said the same thing. There is no equivalence. One is a specific position and an agreement. When a hypothetical position has been put to him, he says it's possible that he may have said the same thing. And then in fairness, if one goes over to page ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, that emerges not from the whole passage. It emerges from nearly two-thirds down the page. The Presiding

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PUTTING TO THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Before the military court and later, before during this court during the investigation and today --" Sorry: "... before this court during the investigation and today, you said that Captain Karanfilov had given you this order." The witness replied: "That's right, that's right." And then the witness adding: "But as I was saying, I'm not ruling out the possibility that I also heard Dragi saying the same thing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is there anything more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it's important, in my submission, that one looks, when one refers to the possibility and an assessment of the way the answer is given, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the possibility was put to the witness by the judge that it was said by Dragi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, the possibility -- what has been put by the judge is, one, that there has been evidence given by another witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I am not excluding any of that. But this witness's evidence was it was Captain Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that's my submission, and that's what I would submit is what he is saying, but the important word, in my submission and I will submit in due course, is, having been given the possibility, accepting the possibility, even if he has no recollection of it, he says, "I am not ruling out the possibility, I also heard Dragi say the same thing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would have thought that that has become very clear in the course of cross-examination and what is apparent from this transcript, and in the course of your re-examination so far. I'm not sure why it is you think that you need to put the whole of this passage to the witness to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am putting it to the witness because -- and as I say, I am not trying to be unkind to my learned friend Mr. Lukic whom I hold in both professional and personal high regard, but in my submission, the way the cross-examination was done, it was done in a way to try and suggest that this witness had said there was an equal likelihood that Vukosavljevic had said it as well as Karanfilov. In my submission, he has never said that in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, as I have indicated earlier, doesn't share that view, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic was cross-examining under some restrictions imposed by the Chamber, and we -- as to how to handle this passage, for obvious reasons. They are reasons which you, on the separate topic, have been very careful to deal with in re-examination, that is distinguishing this witness's actual recollection from what others have put to him. Mr. Lukic was very careful in the way he dealt with it. The point is that what has emerged from that was not, as I understood the witness, an acceptance at all that these were equal possibilities. It was an acceptance that his recollection was of an order from Karanfilov but, as he explained, other things were possible. They included the presence of the soldier Trifunovic at the door of the hangar, although he had no recollection of it. They included that there may have also been a conversation with Vukosavljevic, although he didn't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, that's where the Chamber is, and you are creating a bigger monster to try and destroy it, and the monster, perhaps, is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies. Then I will move on to other topics, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that when you were given the order by Karanfilov, you said that you were bound to obey Karanfilov's orders, namely to withdraw from the prisoners. The question I want to ask you is this: Why were you bound to obey Karanfilov's orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to the first group here. In the first group from the very beginning to the very end, I was there, an order was issued about these prisoners, who was below me, who was above me. On the following day the same officer came, he issued an order to me on that second day, and in my view it was only normal for me to carry out that order. I did not see a single reason for which I should have not carried out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal with cross-examination again. It was during Mr. Lukic's cross-examination. You told us that within the hangar they were pointing at a woman. Now, do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they drew my attention to the fact that there was indeed a woman in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In simple terms, everybody there referred to me as "Captain," because of my rank, and every time I passed by, they wanted to talk to me, they wanted to share with me the information they had. I told them to wait until things settled down. Who it was exactly who told me that there was a woman there, I really don't know. But this is what I remember. I remember that somebody did tell me that there was a woman in the hangar, amongst all these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question is really quite specific. You have said "they" were pointing at a woman, and I'm asking you who are "they"? Is it civilians, is it military? Can you give us an indication of who it was who was pointing at the woman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the policemen who were there. They all wanted to talk to me, they all addressed me as "Captain," but I really can't remember who it was exactly who gave me that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you use the phrase "policemen," is that military policemen or civil policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only military policemen were there. So it was one of my policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, if you have finished that topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me two minutes and I may be able to finish completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be preferable to go over lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friends may be delighted to hear that I have reflected over lunch-time and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's one matter that the Chamber would like some further assistance on. This concerns the evening of the 20th of November when you were at Ovcara. That is the evening when you, on your evidence, were ordered to withdraw your military policemen, and you did. Are you -- what are you able to tell us about the time that you left Ovcara in your three vehicles with your men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the time of day, I really don't know. If I knew when I came there, I would probably know when I went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, are you able, then, to indicate approximately how long you were there that day? How many hours.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trying to do my own math, I think it may have been between an hour and a half and two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that is the -- in your estimate, the total time you spent there; one and a half to two hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to give any approximate indication, either of when you arrived or when you left that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't remember. Not even close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will be pleased to know that's the end of your evidence. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give, and you may now, of course, return to your home and your other activities. The court officer will assist you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we ready for the next witness, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was trying to get that in so that the court officer could hear as he went, that it would speed things up if he brought the next witness in when he returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, and good afternoon to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card that's given to you and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Firstly, may I, with Court's leave, apologise to the witness because he's been here since early this morning. Secondly, what is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragi Vukosavljevic. My father's name was Nastas, my mother's name was Angelina, her maiden name was Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that your date of birth is the 24th of September, 1947; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your ethnic origin is Serbian. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I ask, please, what your current employment is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Currently I work as an engineer in a small company, but usually I act as the general manager of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to deal, if I may, please, with what's called the curriculum vitae of any witness. I think it's right to say that you completed the infantry school for reserve military officers, you were then a commander of a cadet section, and you subsequently became appointed as a commander of a reserve platoon in the JNA of the 80th Infantry, as you describe it, Regiment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a slight correction to make. Before I became company commander, I was also platoon commander for a year. But otherwise, it was as you explained. I spent a year being platoon commander, and then another year being company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, as -- I think as early as 1975 you held the rank of second lieutenant, as you've already told us. You became a company commander, and then I believe also in 1975 you appeared to have completed a course for company commanders in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 1976, is it also correct to say that you were appointed chief of the security organ in the 80th Infantry Regiment and at that time you still had the rank of second lieutenant, although, I think it's right to say that that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- that position normally requires rank of captain first class or major.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again also in 1976 is it right you completed a course for what can be described as the security organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The course for head of security of regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say again that you attended Belgrade University between 1985 and 1986 and you have a degree in -- I think it's called organisation of production processes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was somewhat earlier, though. I graduated from the Belgrade University in 1984, and my title is an engineer for organisation of production processes, is my specialisation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us that you attended a course for security organs. I want to deal with that, if I may, in fairly brief outline. What exactly are the security organs? Can you inform the Court what that means.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I can only speak about that in general terms. I have here a certificate from my government concerning the things that I may address here. Some of the things that we may be referring to would fall into the domain of state security -- state secrets, but the security organs also had to deal with the various issues pertaining to the functioning and security of a given unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That being the case, I would make application that this part of the witness's evidence - and it may become necessary again- be given in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't discern that your question would lead to an answer that would infringe the problem. Did I miss something there, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's difficult to know exactly how far a witness can be constrained if he believes that he is in open session. I do it out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I would press on in open session, but of course if there is some matter you believe involves a state secret, if you would identify that, and we can take special measures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What exactly is the function of the security organ or organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to explain the security organ's work, but I cannot address all the functions pertaining to state security. It is considered a military secret, and is something that is highly confidential. This is the document I received from my government. I haven't been given approval to discuss the work of the State Security Service or its organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, would we be able to deal with areas in general terms without compromising you or state secrets? Could you try and do that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The focus of the work of State Security Service is counter-intelligence work, which also has implications in various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that in 1989, or perhaps 1990, the 80th Infantry Regiment was reformed and it became known as the 80th Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And consequently you became then the chief of the security organ, or perhaps in layman's language, the assistant commander for security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of security organs is the assistant commander for security issues and counter-intelligence service, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I believe as a consequence of that you were promoted to the rank of captain first class, and that was in 1990. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it had nothing to do with my function or title. That was an ordinary promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we can just look at the period prior to 1990, to what extent and how long did you work in what I will call with the regular army as opposed to being involved in any other capacity, for example, reserve?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1989, since I joined the army in 1972, in late November or early December, so I had spent some 17 years up until 1989 with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I think if I just conclude this way, that eventually the affairs were separated again, and this was transformed into the VJ army, and you returned to your old post as chief of security organ of the 80th Infantry Brigade, and that was until 2002 when the brigade itself was disbanded and you were taken off wartime assignment. Is that, in general terms, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps an additional clarification. I was appointed chief of security organ of the 80th Motorised Brigade in 1989 or 1990, and in 1984 or 1985 [as interpreted] there was a transformation unifying the counter-intelligence State Security Service, and for a while I was the head of the state security organ there up until 2002 when the 80th Motorised Brigade was disbanded. Then I was taken off wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see in the translation -- or my attention has been drawn to the fact that line 25, page 66, it seems to be and in 1984 or 1985. 1984, '85. That seems to be out of sequence, whether it's a mistranslation or a misstatement. Can I just read out for the witness's assistance, what has been translated is: "I was appointed chief of the security organ of the 80th Motorised Brigade in 1989 or 1990, and in 1984 or 1985 there was a transformation unifying the counter-intelligence State Security Service." Now, is it 1984, 1985 or '94, '95?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I can address that issue. The services were unified in 1994 or 1995, so the interpretation must have been erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I just want to deal, if I may, please, with the 80th Motorised Brigade. I'll try and deal with it, I hope leading and not in any objectionable way. Is it right that there were two mobilisations of the 80th Motorised Brigade before it was deployed on the 7th of November? The first attempt was in September, 1991, which apparently, to use your phrase, more or less failed when the brigade reached --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- Sid without the 2nd and 3rd Infantry Battalions. And that the second mobilisation was conducted in October or early November, and the brigade was mobilised by battalion, artillery battalion, and independent companies were dispatched in parts of the war zone. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. But we could be more specific, since I participated in all those events, if there is a need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade, by end October, early November, was mobilised. And smaller units that were within the composition of the brigade, being artillery battalions, that was taking place successively. The last part to be mobilised was the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade with staff units. Perhaps I can clarify what those staff units are. That was on the 7th of November. And on the 8th of November, after a short preparation interval in Smederevo, we arrived at Negoslavci in Srem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak directly into the microphone and perhaps move a bit closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if you heard that. The translation booth are having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's splendid. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I doubt if that's a problem. Now, can you tell us, please, what happened to the battalions of the brigade. How were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade had four battalions within its composition. If you'd like me to, later on I can tell you what else it consisted of: One tank battalion and three infantry battalions. The 1st Infantry Battalion was mobilised sometime early in the second half of October and sent off to join the Novi Sad corps. The 2nd Infantry Battalion was mobilised several days after the first battalion. You should have the exact date in the brigade archive. I don't know it off the top of my head right now. It was part of the Guard's Division, and I think Major General Mica Delic was its commander at the time. The 3rd Infantry Battalion was sent to become part of the Guards Motorised Brigade. And that's about it as far as the four battalions are concerned. They were two further battalions, the engineer's battalion and the rear battalion. Those two, the rear battalion was also mobilised on the 7th, the same time as the brigade command. And the engineer's battalion several days earlier. That's all about the battalions; there were a total of six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it right to say that with regard to the 2nd Infantry Battalion, you referred to the Guard's Division, that should not be confused with the Guards Motorised Brigade that was under the command of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we deal with those particular battalions themselves. If we look at the brigade, the 80th Brigade, what was actually left after what I will call, in layman's language, this redeployment or subordination?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the only thing that remained was the rear battalion, some independent companies and the staff command. During the night between the 7th and the 8th of November, a military police platoon was taken out of the -- of its original composition and resubordinated to a different unit that was within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we deal with all the officers of the 80th Motorised Brigade, were they full-time officers, or were they reserve officers, prior to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation took place in late October and early November. All battalion commanders and artillery battalion commanders were full-time military officers. The previous commanders, the reserve commanders, were -- now became their deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with -- and please don't answer this question just yet -- the brigade's light anti-aircraft artillery battalion. I would like to go into closed session for that, or private session, in relation to the reply to that, if you know the name. Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Light anti-aircraft defence, artillery battery, or artillery battalion is a part of the brigade, and it is used for the protection of all of the brigade's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just go into private session in relation to the reply to this question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade, I believe, had an independent military police company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who had command of that company? Do you know his name, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police company was Dragan Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you know how many platoons the company had in --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the company comprised two military police platoons and a traffic platoon, this special subunit. And Vezmarovic also had a company assistant officer, so that's what the military police company comprised, that would be its structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one was assessing the percentage of capacity, would you be able to give an assessment of how up-to-strength they actually were in manpower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: About 70 per cent, manning levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to move on to the topic, if I may, please, I've dealt with it slightly at the beginning, but it's in relation to your duties as a chief of the security organ of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Now, I think it's right to say, and you've already told us that you were the chief during the time, that you were in what I will call the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was chief of the security organ of the 80th Motorised Brigade, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember the date that you came to that particular area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th, on the afternoon of the 8th. I had been mobilised on the 7th, I left Kragujevac from the brigade's assembly place, and on the 8th, on the afternoon of the 8th, I arrived in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when did you actually depart?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: We set out from Kragujevac on the afternoon of the 7th, we spent the night between the 7th and the 8th in Smederevo, and early in the morning on the 8th we eventually left for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you refer to the 7th and the 8th, which month?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: November, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you remember the month that you left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I returned from the front line? Do you mean when the brigade was pulled out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think if you look at my personal military book, the date is the 14th of January. That is when the entire brigade was ordered to pull out. I have this military document on me, I have it in my briefcase. I can show it to you if you like. I may be wrong, give or take a day or two. It's either the 14th or the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that, presumably, is 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. I apologise for being slightly imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think I'm the one who's imprecise most of the time. Now, can we deal, please, with the security department itself. Were there other security officers who assisted you at that time in the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that I had my government's approval to discuss the establishment of the 80th Brigade, I can tell you this: The 80th Brigade comprised seven security officers, including me. Brigade-level security, and that was me, the chief, we had a security officer, a junior officer at that time, and in the 2nd and 3rd Battalion the security officers were also acting as intelligence and security officers at the same time; officers in charge of intelligence and security-related issues. In the rear battalion there was another security officer. He was a security officer and had no intelligence-related duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how many persons were actually subordinated to you within the security organ at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Within the security organ itself I had two officers who were subordinate to me; a full-fledged officer and a non-commissioned officer. In terms of the technical aspects of our work, the battalion security officers were duty-bound to submit reports to me on anything that went on in terms of security in their own units. They were directly linked to battalion commanders. Professionally speaking, or as far as the more technical aspects were concerned, they were linked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you give us the names of the two individuals who were subordinated to you, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Zivko Vasic. He didn't know at the time, but he was already a 2nd lieutenant. They told him later about the promotion. And Mile was a sergeant, but I can't remember his surname. I can't tell you, but it's right there in the brigade archive, the facts should be there, and all his personal information. Should be easy to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. He was later promoted to the rank of Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you ever informed by Colonel Vojnovic to whom your brigade was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, can you please repeat that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you ever informed by Colonel Vojnovic to whom your brigade was subordinated to in early November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of our methodology, the methods we used and in terms of the relationships between the security officers, and the brigade commander, a security officer, as the junior officer, must report to the brigade commander as soon as he arrives. That's what I did. I reported to the brigade commander on the 8th, just upon my arrival in the village of Negoslavci. I asked him to brief me on the brigade's situation, as it was. He gave me whatever information he had but I don't think it was before the 10th that he actually told me that the 80th Motorised Brigade had been resubordinated to the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, which was also the command of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to whom did you start sending your reports vis-a-vis the security organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, a security officer from a subordinate command must report to a security officer from his superior command. The chief of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade at the time was Major Sljivancanin. I think he has since been made into a Colonel, Colonel Sljivancanin. My first meeting with the security officers of the 80th Brigade [as interpreted] occurred in the absence of the chief of the security organ, Mr. Sljivancanin. I hope he doesn't mind me mentioning his name without the rank. The first conversation I had was with Captain Karan, who was with the security organ in Osijek, but he was now with the Guard's Motorised Brigade in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The questions that I -- or the question that I asked you is to whom did you start sending your reports vis-a-vis the security organ? Sorry, I just want to deal with what might be a misinterpretation, because I'm looking specifically at line 13 -- page 75, 13. So that is why I put the question and the, answer to see whether it needs clarifying, whether it is an error, or whether it's a mistranslation. I am entirely in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the question that I asked you, but the answer that we have got -- part of it, if I may say, is: "My first meeting with the security officers of the 80th Brigade occurred in the absence of the chief of the security organ, Mr. Sljivancanin." Now, you say "officers of the 80th Brigade." Is that a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It must be either a misinterpretation -- As far as I remember, I said security officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade. I was an officer from a subordinate command, and my duty was to report to the security officers of my superior command, which was precisely what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you for clarifying that. Now, did you actually visit the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade by virtue of your duty --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And to whom did you report or to whom did you see -- whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, I'm not sure if it's been interpreted, but the first person I met was Captain First Class Karan, who was a clerk with the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time see Lieutenant Karanfilov in the execution of your duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see him a number of times. But the first meeting I had with any of them was the meeting I had with Mr. Captain First Class Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with Lieutenant Karanfilov. In relation to your dealings with him, to whom was he subordinated? Are you able to say? Or who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, Lieutenant Karanfilov was a security officer of the counter-intelligence group of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and was subordinated to Mr. Sljivancanin, who was the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how often did you visit the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: One could say almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How important was it at that time for a close contact with the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade vis-a-vis the cooperation between the 80th Brigade and the Guards Motorised Brigade or OG South?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, if there was a higher degree or extent of cooperation, results were better. However, the same applies as I answered to your previous question: The 80th Motorised Brigade did not have any considerable forces at its disposal, so the degree of interest of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade, to me, as its chief, was perfectly in keeping with what the brigade had in terms of its capacity or the extent to which problems regarding security were current at all. You might say not considerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To what extent must a senior officer be appraised of what I will call day to day security considerations within the security organ itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, he must be appraised of all the important details that may or may not occur in any of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one deals with your experience as a soldier, what was the overall impression that you had of the security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade with regard to their professionalism and the way they approached their work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a thankless task for me as a reserve officer to pass judgement on these top-level professionals who worked as security officers for the Guards Brigade. For the most part those were hand-picked officers, as it were; the cream of the crop, top-level professionals, top-notch men. That's at least what I believe. It is, however, a thankless task for me to pass judgement on officers who have a much higher degree of both education and training than I do myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with reports, both in oral and written form. Was there any obligation - perhaps I'll use the word "duty" - to submit written reports on a regular basis? If there was, can you tell us to what extent and to whom you would send those reports.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In principle the form the reporting took would be agreed on by the security officers of the subordinate and the superior commands. For the most parts, reports up the chain of command were oral. I think there were a couple of written reports about security problems arising in the 80th Brigade. They were low on manpower, and low on units in terms of what they had under their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I may come back to this topic in due course, but I would like to deal, if I may, please, with what I will call the local Serb TO, or sometimes known as volunteers or paramilitaries. Do you know, or can you remember who was the commander of the local Serb TO in Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My first contact with any civilian bodies or TO units occurred just after the 80th Motorised Brigade had entered Vukovar. All I can talk about is the -- is that time period and from this point onwards, but if you want me to tell you specifically, I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There may be a problem on the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I apologise to my learned friend, but I would like to say something about the way he phrased the previous question. I don't think it is something that arises from what we have heard so far, but on page 78, line 20, he chose to speak about "the local Serb TO, sometimes known as volunteers or paramilitaries." I don't think those two terms should be set on an equal footing, as it were, and this comes across as being suggested by my learned friend's question, which may eventually lead to confusing the witness, and we wish to avoid that, don't we.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you like to tell us the term that you believe is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I could possibly be confused by a question like this. The TO, the volunteers and the paramilitaries, those are three different categories. In the former Yugoslavia the Territorial Defence was organised much as a military unit, at a territorial level. Each region, each municipality had a TO staff. Depending on the size of the respective socio-political community, and I mean the region or the area, its TO would be set up. This applied to the republican level too. Paramilitaries are paramilitaries. We all know what that means, don't we. Volunteers are volunteers. Under the principle of unity of command, all units happening to be in an area where the JNA are carrying out their operations are expected to submit themselves to the Supreme Command of the JNA and to the JNA units. We have here the TO, which was set up along the same lines, basically, as the JNA itself. They had the same sort of command structure: Squad, detachment, battalion, that sort of thing. Sir, is that a satisfactory explanation for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And did you know the names of the leaders of the -- what I will call the local TO in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the 23rd I had contacts with representatives of the local Territorial Defence. The commander of the Territorial Defence, which was not your question, but if you want me to, I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence was Miroljub Vujovic, the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence was Stanko Vujanovic, and those were two key figures in the Territorial Defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever know one person called Milan Lancuzanin within the context of the Vukovar TO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He was the commander of the Leva Supoderica detachment, and his nickname was Kameni. He was also known as Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To whom were the local Vukovar TO subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the 80th Brigade entered Vukovar, which was on the 23rd, 24th or on 25th - I can't be sure of the exact date, but there are documents testifying to that. All the units that were present in the territory of Vukovar had to be subordinated to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we deal with the period 8th, 9th, 10th of November, do you know to whom they were subordinated at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. At the time I was in the territory, however not a single unit of the 80th Brigade was in contact with those units. However, all those units had to be subordinated to one of the commands of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to which command of the JNA did you believe that they were subordinated to at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In my view, they should have been subordinated to the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, but I'm not positive about that. I can't be sure whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to deal, then, with the individuals to whom you have been referring. You have told us about Kameni. Were you aware, or did you form any view, in respect of his political ideas or sympathies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Truth be told, I did speak to this person several times, and I believe that he was inclined towards the radicals, but at that time the JNA did not attach too much importance to the -- to any ideology. Patriotism was of more importance, and the fact that people were either interested or not in becoming members of the JNA. That was what was important at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal with the Petrova Gora, the detachment or the TO detachment, as it's sometimes called. Do you know if it continued to exist after the 80th Motorised Brigade entered Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Petrova Gora detachment was [indiscernible], Vukovar no longer existed. The only thing that existed was the Leva Supoderica detachment, and its commander was Mr. Milan Lancuzanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I think there is a concern that perhaps when we mentioned the days, the 23rd, 24th and 25th, I presume we're talking about November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, sir. I apologise, I thought that this went without saying. Can you please remind me when you want me to be specific about any dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite sure the dates now will be set in stone, at least for the month. Now, may I deal, please, with regard to the nature of the uniform of the local TO. Are you able to assist us on that? What way did they tend to dress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the uniforms of the TO, those uniforms differed. They varied. They wore JNA uniforms as a matter of principle. There was the M-77 uniform, but there were also camouflage uniforms; M-89 or M-90. As for the type of uniform, it depended on the place in the hierarchy of the TO. Those who were high-ranking had more complete uniforms than the mere foot soldiers. In any case, they had JNA hats, coats, trousers, they also wore sneakers and other types of blouses and trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to deal with the -- Major Sljivancanin in very brief order. I think it's right to say that you believe that you met him on two or three occasions, in Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you met him socially. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not socially. Just in my official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the way it was phrased. But is it correct to say that he showed you an element of courtesy when it came to dealing with you, that he was polite and courteous?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Very much so. Very polite, very courteous. A good colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When I meant socially - perhaps it was an imprecise question - that if you had informal talks with him, he would, for example, always offer you a drink?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The first time I met with Mr. -- Major Sljivancanin, he welcomed me, he inquired after my health, my family, he offered me his telephone to call home, he told me that they had a bathroom if I wanted to take a bath. He did offer me a drink. In other words, he was a very polite, the meeting was very cordial, and the cordiality was very much typical of the people who hail from Serbia, from Sumadija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect there will be a few people in this court who will be glad to hear that. Let's move on, if I may. Can I deal, though, with what I will call work-related issues. If you did ever speak to him about a work-related issue, did he deal with it himself, or how did he deal with it, if not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the training that I underwent as a security man, I can say that when I arrived in the combat area I had to be briefed about the security situation, and in that sense I asked Major Sljivancanin to brief me. However, he mostly referred me to Captain Karan, who was the security organ in the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one was dealing with what I will call training for security organs, is there a -- a belief where the security organ should be located when one refers to a front line or a headquarters? Was there any particular philosophy in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, a security organ, and not only security organs, but all the organs of the command, have to be at the disposal of the brigade commander at all times. They have to provide him with proposals in order to help him in the decision-making process when it came to the use of subordinated units. The chief of security is supposed to be in the brigade command. However, the work of the security organ requires a lot of field work as well. And since you have given me the green light to talk about the organisation structure of the motorised brigade, I can say that I had two officers to work in the divisions where there were no security organs and I directly contacted the two of them and the four security organs in the battalions that I have mentioned here; the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, and the rear battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with Major Sljivancanin. You have said that he was head of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is what I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Within the confines of OG South, who was Major Sljivancanin's commander? To whom did he advise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the chain of command, the brigade commander is superior to the security organs in any of the brigades and according to the professional line, the security organs are linked to the security organs of the superior command. And the superior command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, I don't know which command it was, I can't be sure of that. And that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one takes Colonel Mrksic, what relationship or what role did Major Sljivancanin play in respect of him within what I will call a professional capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about professional links, and you are obviously referring to the counter-intelligence, that is something that the security organ is in charge of, I can answer you that, but can you just please confirm that this is what you're referring to in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's part of what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to counter-intelligence, the security organ reports to his commander, either me or Major Sljivancanin. The security organ has to provide them with the most important thing that jeopardised the work of the unit. I did that, and according to the command chain, both him and I report to the brigade commander who gives us tasks, but we also are given tasks by the security organ of our superior command at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one takes Colonel Mrksic, one takes Major Sljivancanin, what role does Major Sljivancanin play vis-a-vis his -- what role does Major Sljivancanin play in respect of Colonel Mrksic's capacity as commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He had to inform him about the security situation in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say "security situation of the unit," when you refer to "unit," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Guards Motorised Brigade and all the units subordinated to the Guards Motorised Brigade, which was at the same time the command of the OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how important a task is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to exaggerate the role of the security organ, but at some moments this role is crucial. The information that a security organ can provide his commander with can help him resolve many things and provide for the correct and appropriate use of his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me give you a situation. If it became apparent that units subordinated to eventually Colonel Mrksic was behaving in a way that clearly was either threatening the security of the unit or was behaving in a way that would create significant problems for the unit, and Major Sljivancanin was aware of that, what obligation would he have to inform Colonel Mrksic of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: To inform him fully. The information that flows between the security organ and the commander is specified: The chief of security strives to inform the commander on any of the security issues as soon as possible, in the briefest possible time. And commander in his turn can ask for additional information and additional explanation, based on which eventually he will make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, what I would like to do is I want to deal with what I will use the generic head of evacuations. At the time that you were in Vukovar, were you involved in any evacuations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Not in the classical sense of the word. Not any evacuations from the beginning to the end. However, I participated in providing security for the prisoners of war who had been taken to the Mitnica sector. Any evacuation starts at the moment when prisoners of war were received, and it ends when the prisoners of war are taken to a certain destination or to a sector where they are guarded and secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which units are deemed to be the most suitable for guarding or securing prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The military police units, which were best equipped for guarding prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why is it that the military police units are the most suitable for guarding or securing prisoners of war? Can you explain why it is that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Because they have to undergo special training. They are trained to prevent any riots, they are trained to provide security for facilities, they know how to treat prisoners of war, that's why they are best suited to provide security for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How normal, or is it a normal procedure for a security officer to be in charge of an evacuation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is not within the purview of a security officer, as far as I know. A security officer can be consulted vis-a-vis an evacuation. However, when it comes to the operations on the ground, guarding and providing security, this is within the purview of the security subject's commanders and units subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one deals with Territorial Defence units, in your professional judgement, at the end of a conflict, how prudent or wise is it for a Territorial Defence unit to be involved in an evacuation operation exclusively?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the assessment of the commander. It is up to the commander to decide on that. And the assessment is based on the information provided to him by his subordinates. Any operation is based on such information, any operation, including an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again within your professional evaluation, if there was information available to that commander that local TO units had been committing atrocities or had been harming prisoners, would it be, in your judgement, advisable or wise for local TO units to be subsequently involved in an evacuation of similar prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Of course not. And I have a request from you, Mr. Moore. I am an engineer and when you ask me for my professional opinion, you are actually asking for my opinion as a reserve security officer, and my profession is somewhat different. And I apologise for this slight correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is not a problem at all. We will deal with it in other ways as well. Let us move on, then, to evacuations that you were aware of in the Vukovar area. Were you aware of -- what was the first evacuation that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The first evacuation that I became aware of, i.e., that I saw, was a convoy of buses that passed through Negoslavci from the direction of Vukovar. When I asked what this was all about, I was told that those were Croatian prisoners of war, members of various military formations, like the Guards, and so on and so forth. They were taken in buses through Negoslavci and, as far as I could understand, they were taken to the detention unit in Sremska Mitrovica. The second evacuation that I am aware of was the evacuation of the Mitnica group. I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not a problem. We deal with the first evacuation. We use the phrase in English members of various military formations like the guards. Now, "guards," in English, can mean guards as in prison guards, or security guards, or of course in this instance, it can mean the military guards regiment.
