So we've got a translation, "various military formations like the Guards." What do you mean by that? Can you be a little more specific? It's just a question of language here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, in Vukovar there were units of the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, and they were referred to as Guards or ZNG soldiers. They were members of the Croatian Defence Council, which was the term used for the Croatian military. And they were also MUP members. The buses that I mentioned that went from Borovo Naselje through Negoslavci and further on to Sremska Mitrovica, carried members of those formations that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that is your first evacuation. The second, you were going to tell us, related to Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But might I just respectfully inquire if the Court is seeking an adjournment, as I think you normally do, within an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it's convenient, then, Mr. Moore, we can break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's just I was going to start Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, there is only three minutes, so, yes. We will have the first break now and resume at 20 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, then with Mitnica. You have said you were going to tell us about the Mitnica evacuation. Now, how did you become involved with that, please, or how did you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I got involved with that pursuant to orders by my brigade commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Some forces of the 80th Motorised Brigade were sent with me, the assignment being to provide security for the prisoners, but companies of the military police, brigade command officers, and people from the staff units were charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you actually arrive, or did you go to Ovcara on the 18th in relation to the Mitnica evacuation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in what capacity were you involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As a security officer. That was my basic assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what specifically was your task or role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The role of a security officer in providing security for and guarding POWs should be none at all, in fact. I suppose the brigade commander sent me there to monitor what was going on and to make sure that the prisoners were being treated in keeping with the Geneva and Hague conventions, whether the procedure being applied was proper. Otherwise, he should not have got me involved at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the name of the brigade commander who sent you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We know from evidence that has given before the Court that the Mitnica evacuation came to Ovcara on the 18th and departed on the 19th of November. Did you remain at Ovcara through the night and early morning of the 18th, 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I can provide a detailed description of the security regime, if you want to know about that, if it is of any interest to the Chamber or any other gentlemen present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's exactly my next question. Would you be kind enough, please, to tell us, using your words, what the security regime that existed for those prisoners involved.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: We set up two security systems. External security around the hangar at Ovcara, where the captured members of what I will call the Croatian armed forces were, the ZNG, the police, and all the rest that I mentioned. We had two security systems, the external one and the internal one. From the direction of the Bulgarian cemetery and the forest of Djerga, there was still sporadic shooting. That was one of the reasons. We provided external security by using members of the staff units. The signals company, the ABHO, the staff command, the reconnaissance company had been taken away, and had been sent to guard the observation post, the artillery observation post. Internal security comprised members of the military police and officers from the brigade command. We worked in two shifts. One shift would relieve the other. Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, the Chief of Staff, was in charge of the operation. He, myself, and Captain Vezmarovic stayed until the next morning. I was so tired, however, that just before the prisoners were put on buses I had been sent back to the command to get some rest by the commander. And that was about it. We offered the commander water, food, and he wanted to have some food -- some water. We used jerry cans, 50-litre jerry cans, and we brought water two or three times; there were 200 people there, after all. This would be a detailed description, but if you want more on any of the various aspects of the situation, I can provide that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wasn't intending to ask you any additional details. But how many individuals, from your recollection, were actually used to guard the Mitnica group of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: A single shift would normally comprise between 40 and 50, which adds up to a total of about 100 soldiers for both shifts. But this is a very liberal estimate, and this was, after all, 16 years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told by the interpreters if you could keep your voice up, as you speak quite slowly and quietly. Why is it necessary to work in shifts when you are providing security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Because of the exhaustion. Under the rules, a shift should last for two hours, and then the soldiers on guard should be relieved. But we took six-hour shifts. Our soldiers had six-hour shifts. Is it any better now, in terms of the audibility of my voice, and the pace?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is, thank you very much. That's extremely helpful. Can you -- you've already told us about Vezmarovic. Do you know if Karanfilov was present at any time during the Mitnica evacuation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was, and he was practically the one who brought the command of the Mitnica group. We were there, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, I was there, perhaps there were other officers there, but I don't remember. Captain Karanfilov practically brought the group there, as well as the commander of the group, Filip Karaula. We talked to him, we told him about the security regime, what it would be inside the hangar, which steps would be taken, and his attention was drawn to the fact that they were to -- expected to abide by this, otherwise we might be compelled to take steps of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, what was Karanfilov's role in the Mitnica evacuation, either on the 18th or the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll put it this way: I was entirely unfamiliar with his role in the evacuation of Mitnica, but we saw him that evening, and he handed the group over. He kept mentioning The Hague conventions, he offered the prisoners a separate room, all the conditions enshrined in The Hague conventions for the treatment of military officers, but I didn't know his role, I had not been aware of his role up to the moment we actually met at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember if you saw him on the 19th in relation to Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Mitnica group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't see him. But I may have left a little earlier, just before they started putting prisoners on the buses there. Maybe someone else saw him. I know that my brigade came to visit us that morning, and the commander sent me off to get some rest. He realised that I was very tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have spoken about your fatigue level. Vezmarovic was clearly there as well. In which capacity was he employed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He is a captain, he was the military police company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you describe your own fatigue level. Was that a consequence of the guard duty that you had whilst at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: You could put it that way. Although in those days I got very little sleep, and I ate too little. I had a muscle inflammation as well, I was suffering muscle inflammation in those days. I had not adapted quickly enough to conditions of war. I used to work as a manager before that, you see, so my physical fitness levels were not perhaps what you would expect in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we also deal, then, please, with whether you can recollect if there were any incidents that caught your attention through the night and early morning of 18th and 19th of November at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, as for any incidents that could have affected the security situation, there were none. There were some marginal things happening. Some people came over from Vukovar to see who was there. There was a lieutenant-colonel from the Guards Brigade [Realtime transcript read in error "Brigade"]. He was probably the chief from one or the other branches, and he wanted to get inside, but we sent him away, we turned him away. But there were no incidents affecting the prisoners' safety or the security regime around the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal with the matter or incident in respect of the lieutenant-colonel from the -- I thought you had said the Guards Brigade. I've only got on the translation, "Brigade." Is that correct or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade, yes. I used to see that man whenever I went to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we deal with the incident involving the lieutenant-colonel of the Guards Brigade. What exactly did he do that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He wanted to get inside and see the POWs. Not sure what his intention was. He was slightly under the influence, so I turned him away. It was a risk I was not prepared to run. I used the assistance of some military police officers there, so we just sent him packing in a Pinzgauer -- or rather, I apologise, in a Puch, because that's how he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did he demonstrate a friendly attitude towards the prisoners of war or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. He was inebriated, you see. It's very difficult to judge a man like that. And he was acting as someone who had probably had a drop too many, as they say. He never got in touch physically with any of the POWs, not enough for him to display clearly what his attitude or intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal, then, please, with -- you've told us about the Mitnica evacuation. I think it's right to say that you did not take any part in the hand-over and evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you did not go to the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I would like to deal, if I may, please, with the 20th of November, and I will start in the afternoon of that day. Did there come a time when you were contacted by one of your -- or your commander, Colonel Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that was at dusk. I could hardly call that afternoon. The Serbs usually considered the afternoon hours to be between noon and dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The Irish perhaps sometimes a little differently. But in any event, what location was that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Not that I can hold it against anyone, especially not against the Irish. This was at the command of the 80th Brigade, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did Vojnovic say to you, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Vojnovic gave me an order that was rather imprecise. He said there's some sort of a mess going on at Ovcara, here is my vehicle, take two officers from the brigade command, and see what's going on and what can be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, was -- was Vojnovic, or had Vojnovic been notified that there was going to be individuals or individuals at Ovcara on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about that. It's not something that I can speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So did you do as you were ordered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It was a commander's order, and one had to carry that sort of thing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went to Ovcara, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at Ovcara I found a rather large number of people outside the hangar. Assembled, if you like, outside the hangar. They stood in the way, keeping me from accessing the hangar. They wanted to know what the JNA were doing there at all because these were POWs who had surrendered to them, they said. They were their POWs, they said, not the JNA's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you refer to the phrase "rather a large number of people," can we estimate, or are you able to estimate the number of people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, and it has been a long time, after all, it's been 16 years, I reckon 300 people, possibly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to see if any of them were armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: All were. All were. For the most part they were carrying rifles, automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs, but there were a number of trophy weapons too, Thompsons, semi-automatic rifles, but those were more up-to-date, they weren't trophy weapons, and there were some M-53 machine-guns too. Machine-guns, automatic rifles, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, are you able to say if any of them were wearing uniforms or military dress?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes. They were wearing uniforms. And I think when I spoke about the TO members earlier on I described that but I can go through that again, I can cover that ground again if you'd like me to. It's the same old story; it was a combination of different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, you needn't go through it again, for me, anyway. And how would you describe, painting a verbal picture, how would you describe the atmosphere of that crowd outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, I only stayed there briefly. My take on the situation was that the situation was a rather complex one. The authority of the military police and the JNA was not being obeyed by those people who were armed. They just wanted to get at the prisoners and take them under their wing, as it were. So they were pushing and shoving, trying to interpose themselves, as it were, between members of the 80th Brigade, some of them police officers, some of them from the staff units, with the obvious intention of taking charge of the prisoners themselves. I asked Captain Vezmarovic what this was about. And he said, well, you know, we're facing a great amount of problems there, I can't keep them out of the hangar, they want to get at the prisoners of war. There were threats being uttered. Threats along the lines of execution and so on and so forth. So my assessment was the situation was getting out of control, and the JNA people there were no longer able to safeguard order inside the hangar. But there were no guards outside, as far as the JNA were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to assess your own personal safety -- or how did you assess your personal safety at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't at a desirable level, but if one is involved in a war, you have to have all possibilities in mind. All of us who were members of the armed forces have given an oath stating that we would even put our own lives at risk, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you consider there was a -- that your life might have been at risk if things turned for the worst?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In case the armed people who were there, in case they took over control, I would have done my utmost to try and prevent that. Up to the level of using my firearm, which would in turn result in my loss of life. There were very few of us from the JNA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you consider that a possibility at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was an option. But one tries to avoid that, and one tries to adjust to the situation at the given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Ovcara on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: For about 10 minutes. Maybe a couple of minutes more. The time I needed to see what the situation was, and as I found it quite delicate, I thought it better to go and see my superior commander to try and gain some time and undertake measures in order to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether Vezmarovic, who was there, or indeed any others, whether they had radios available to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. As for the 80th Brigade, the equipment communications were almost non-existent. There was some sort of a radio communication, but silence was being imposed, there was a ban, and they couldn't use their radios. They used telephone links for as long as they could at wartime, but there was no telephone connection between, say, Ovcara and the 80th Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So where did you return to, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the 80th Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where was that located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Negoslavci. Those were three houses at the very end of the village, and that's where the brigade command was. To be more specific, it was the second house from the end where the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It may be my error, but did you leave any persons -- you say that you travelled to Ovcara. Did you leave any of the people that you travelled with at Ovcara whilst you were went back to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two officers with me. Both captains first class, Dacic and Vukic. One was head of engineers and one head of the ABHO department. They were there, I left them there, thinking it was better for me to do that, to increase the number of the JNA members there, although I had to return on my own. I was alone with the driver, and I wasn't happy about that. In any case, they remained behind, whereas I returned to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with your return to Negoslavci and the brigade command. When you went to the actual brigade command location, was Vojnovic there or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. He wasn't at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you inquire where he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the brigade there was always a duty officer or a duty group. And the commander has to tell where he was to be found. I was told he was at the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade in Negoslavci. I apologise again. Am I loud enough now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your voice all the time tends to be very quiet. I think we need to get you back into the habit of some parade ground voice. It would help if you could keep your voice pitched louder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So let us deal, then, please, you say that he was not at the brigade command, and you were told he was at the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade in Negoslavci. So did you go to the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, to try and find the brigade commander to inform him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you locate him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In a way, yes. He was in a meeting with the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade. I was told that by the non-commissioned officer who was there in front of the meeting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Mile Mrksic. At that time he was still Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you try and gain entrance to speak to Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to ask for instruction from the Chamber. Perhaps I needn't speak more loudly, but volume could be put up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By and large the volume is set at an automatic pre-set level. You mean you can't hear yourself? That can be adjusted, and the court officer will now adjust your own volume. Our problem is, we can't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On occasion I can't hear myself speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's got a lot to do with your voice level rather than the system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is louder now. I can hear everything much better. This was the usher's proper reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we just return, please, to your evidence. You were told that Mrksic was in a meeting with -- with Vojnovic. And you were told that by the non-commissioned officer who was there in front of the meeting room. Now, did you ask to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you ask to speak to Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Security organs have priority in approaching commanders to report on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you then gain access to Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Not for the first hour or an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you inform the non-commissioned officer that you had important information for Vojnovic or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. I've also stated that I was from the security organ, and that I had some urgent information for Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you recollect if that non-commissioned officer interrupted or went inside and interrupted the meeting with Mrksic and Vojnovic or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He told me he was ordered expressly not to interrupt the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to my learned friend. The way he put his last question, I don't think that arises from some of the previous answers. There my learned friend asked whether the non-commissioned officer interrupted or went inside to interrupt the meeting with Mrksic and Vojnovic. I don't think the witness ever said that the meeting included only Mrksic and Vojnovic. Perhaps my learned friend could explore more on the nature of the meeting and then to resort to such questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The meeting hasn't been explored at all. We were told of two people in there, so I don't think there is fault with the question, Mr. Vasic. But if that matter isn't developed, you may do so, of course, in your cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us earlier on that you did not gain access to Vojnovic, the phrase was "not for the first hour or an hour and a half." So can we deal then, please, when you actually did manage to speak to Vojnovic. When and where did you speak to him, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in front of the meeting room. That was in the duration of one or one and a half hours. It was quite a long time, and it can cost you a battle. I'm not sure whether it was an hour or an hour and a half, but that's when I finally managed to see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic and I reported on the situation the way I described here when answering your questions. In principle a security organ or person from a security organ shouldn't waste the commander's time. You have four or five minutes to use to report on everything, and then you must wait for the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you spoke or informed Vojnovic of the situation that you have described here in court. Did Vojnovic react in any way to the information that you gave him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He reacted -- well, I don't want to say he was afraid. He is a soldier, still, but he was somewhat at a loss. He asked, well, what are we to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he indicate whether he had been speaking to Colonel Mrksic about the -- what I will call the Ovcara situation, prior to speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that during the briefing with Colonel Mrksic he expressed -- explained the situation at Ovcara and that there were armed people there, that the situation was on the verge of an incident, but he also stated that he received no reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Having informed -- Witness, could you just please keep your eyes straight ahead with the learned judges. Thank you very much, indeed. Now, in relation to the conversation that you have had with Vojnovic, and you have said he looked not afraid but slightly perplexed or surprised, what then happened between yourself and Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you chose a far better word than I did. He was perplexed, indeed. Well, he said -- well, at the time we addressed each other as comrades, and he said, well, let's speak to Comrade Mrksic and see what we are to do about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you speak to Comrade Mrksic, as suggested by Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Colonel Vojnovic asked me to report on the matter, although it was not the usual practice. A junior officer is never to submit a report in the presence of a senior one. But he asked me to do so, and I have explained to Lieutenant-General Mrksic the way I did to Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did you tell Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the way a report of a security organ to the commander needs to be short, brief, and to the point, as for the basic security issue at hand. I expressed that as briefly as I could, but now 16 years later, please don't ask me to repeat that word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will not ask you to repeat it word for word, but I will ask you, please, to summarise or recollect what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I said, that there was a group of armed people there, stating that those POWs belonged to them, that they were inebriated and that they behaved threateningly towards the prisoners and that they showed no respect whatsoever as regards the members of the JNA who were there; in this case, those people were from the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did Mrksic reply?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not to me. After a short while, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic asked him, Colonel, sir, what are we to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you carry on, please, with the account as you are giving it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, as I have already told you, that in the presence of a superior officer a younger officer should not say much. I submitted my report, and then I kept quiet. And then lieutenant-colonel asked the colonel what to do. The colonel was a bit angry, and he reacted rather angrily. He asked why we were reporting to him on this, because he didn't have the time to deal with that. Something along these lines. And since the discussion between the two officers superior to me assumed a different tone, I believed it appropriate for me to withdraw a little and give them space to deal with the problem. They started walking away from me, and some three or four minutes later Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic returned and asked me to go and to convey an order to the members of the 80th Brigade to withdraw from Ovcara. Since I didn't have a vehicle, he provided me with his staff vehicle, Fiat Campagnola, and in that vehicle I returned to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to deal with one or two matters, if I may. You have told us that Colonel Mrksic was a bit angry and he reacted rather angrily. Now, was there any reference or inquiry to why the 80th Motorised Brigade was at Ovcara at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The lieutenant-colonel and the colonel did discuss that, but, after a lapse of time, it's very difficult for me to remember what they said. And also, I was at a certain distance from them and I didn't hear the actual conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the conversation between Mrksic and Vojnovic, as far as you could see, being in the same room, who dominated the conversation? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the most superior is also the dominant one. That is always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that the case here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were given the order or instruction by Vojnovic to return to Ovcara and withdraw the protecting unit there, when that was said to you, was that in the same room where the conversation had occurred between Mrksic and Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when Vojnovic spoke to you, in what tone of voice did he use? Was it whisper, loud, shout? Can you give us an indication, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He used a normal tone of voice. His behaviour was normal. Vojnovic is a very good officer, in my view. And his attitude towards the security organ is the one of respect. That is always the case, because if they don't respect each other, they cannot cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were there other members or individuals in the room when Vojnovic and yourself were giving this report to Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a non-commissioned officer that I have already mentioned, and there were also two or three armed military policemen who provided security for the meeting room. There must have been some other officers who had left the room before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Mrksic remain in the room, or indeed at the headquarters at that time, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that General Mrksic did start leaving, and that Vojnovic escorted him. Vojnovic then returned to talk to me and the general proceeded on his way. I can't tell you exactly where he went, but he went towards the far corner of that room. Maybe there was a door there or something, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us that you then were allowed to use the vehicle, I think it's a Campagnola, to go back to Ovcara. Now, may I deal, please, with the trip back to Ovcara. It's 16 or 15 years now, but how long did it take you to get back to Ovcara? Can you remember, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the village of Negoslavci is rather long. I believe that its length is between four and five kilometres altogether. And we had to drive rather slowly, the roads could have been mined, and since there was just me and my driver in the vehicle, the driver was in a state of panic. He drove slowly, and I believe that we travelled the distance of four or five kilometres as long as half an hour. It must have been half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you got back to Ovcara, did you see Vezmarovic there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Vezmarovic and I saw the two officers that had come to me, they had already abandoned the hangar. There were also three Pinzgauer vehicles there, and as I was leaving they returned towards Ovcara, and when I returned, they returned towards the road leading to Negoslavci, and the troops -- actually the military policemen and officers were getting ready to leave, to get into the vehicles and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You had been told, or ordered, by Vojnovic to order Vezmarovic and the soldiers there to withdraw. Now here is a situation where they seem to be already in the process of withdrawing prior to your arrival. Did you ever -- or did you inquire how it was they were getting ready to leave, what had caused them to leave prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you said that I was the one who ordered Vezmarovic, that Vojnovic asked me to order Vezmarovic to withdraw. According to the rules of service, the work of the security organ is such that they do not have the right to issue orders to the military police. I could not issue an order to Captain Vezmarovic, I could only convey a lieutenant-colonel's order, and he was then supposed to carry that order out. In other words, no security organ has an order-issuing role, and this is specified in the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question was, did you inquire or did you find out why it was that the military police and Vezmarovic were in the process of leaving prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not ask anybody anything. I can't even remember whether I conveyed lieutenant-colonel's order to him, because he had already started acting in the spirit of what I was supposed to convey to him. It is possible that captain had been informed in some other way. As I said here, I cannot provide you anything more precise about that, I cannot be of any more assistance to the Trial Chamber with that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you not ask Vezmarovic, Why are you leaving at this time? Because when you had left, he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific when you ask me this. I said that he already acted in the spirit of the order issued by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic that I was supposed to convey to him. And there was no reason for me to ask him anything, because he had already acted in accordance with the order that I was supposed to convey. We may have spoken about that; you should ask him. But I really can't remember that we ever discussed that. I can't remember any such conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We've already heard evidence on that and I can move on to other topics. Let us deal, then, please, with the situation at Ovcara. Did you see, then, Vezmarovic and the military policemen leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I did not hear the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Vezmarovic and the military policemen leave Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I left together with them in the Fiat Campagnola vehicle, together with the two officers, Vukic and Dacic, the two who had come with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you left, were there still armed men outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Even more of them were there than when I arrived there the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, were those individuals outside the hangar, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to wearing uniforms, did you see uniforms of those people outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already described their uniforms. You asked me the same thing in relation to my first arrival there. If you want me to repeat, I will. I'll gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, you also replied to us that there were additional people who had arrived and was a larger crowd than before. I just wish to clarify in relation to the new situation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Right. The situation was the same. There were all sorts of uniforms, the uniforms varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember if you entered the hangar on this second occasion when you returned to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. There was no need for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at Ovcara prior to leaving?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: 10 minutes or so. No longer than it took the two officers who had come with me to get into the vehicle. Maybe even less time than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you return to, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I returned to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you speak to Colonel Vojnovic upon your return?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did. I briefed him, I told him that the task had been accomplished in the spirit of his order. I believe that Vezmarovic had told him the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to new topics. I know we are at four minutes before time, but it is a natural break for a witness, and indeed myself, when giving evidence, and I would ask the Court to adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now for the evening and resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.26 p.m.,
